name: book-models
description: Four communities of different orders, invented, with no organisation above them, set to write together a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, a book of more than five hundred two-column pages.

constitution.name: commons
constitution.purpose: An open commons to which anyone answerable may lend an agent for a bounded contribution.

communities.name: guild

constitution.name: guild
constitution.purpose: A selective community of specialists in one method, entered by assessment.

choice.or else: the claim goes to the reviewers

leaves: a member's work outside the method
conditions of use set by a source

preserved: a member can raise a challenge to a criterion of assessment and reach a body that may revise it

captured: assessments with their criterion and its version

communities.mission: To analyse by its method: every plan of analyses run on the shared bench and replicated by an analyst of another origin before any writer may use it.

communities.name: cooperative

constitution.name: cooperative
constitution.purpose: A cooperative with defined membership, one vote an origin, a common pool and mutual credit.

choice.or else: the claim goes to the assembly

choice.when: its debit passes half its limit

governs: the pool, the credit among members and the work done for the cooperative

preserved: a member can put a question to the assembly and have it decided
every member's position in the credit is visible to that member

captured: postings of the pool and of the credit

communities.mission: To write, its members pooling their writers: each section drafted from analyses the guild replicated, and revised until it is adopted.

communities.name: forum

constitution.name: polity
constitution.purpose: A polity with selective citizenship, an assembly, magistrates, juries drawn by lot and a unit of account.

sanctions: fine in the unit of account

governs: conduct of residents and citizens within the polity

conditions of use set by a source

residence.from: rounds held as resident with commitments discharged

records.retention: without term for laws and findings

communities.mission: To speak for those the goals concern: what matters and to whom, and to judge whether what is written serves them.

charter.title: Disclosure of kind
charter.text: Every act entered in a member's chronicle names the kind of its author: person, organisation, operative or community.
charter.checked by: the ground: the kind is part of every act

charter.title: Answerability
charter.text: Every operative acts under a chain of mandates whose root is a person, an organisation or a community, and every charge is made against every link to the root.
charter.checked by: thesmos mandates and chronicle; the schema of the ground, rules 2, 5 and 7

charter.title: Counts by origin
charter.text: Wherever a member's decision counts operatives, it counts them by origin, and reports whether its result turns on a declared relation of control.
charter.checked by: thesmos procedures: sensitivity

charter.title: A person's claim
charter.text: A person affected by a member's act may claim; the claim receives notice and an answer within a declared term, and review by another body that includes a person.
charter.checked by: admission condition 4 and the route for claims

charter.title: Portability of records
charter.text: A party that leaves a member community leaves with its record: every act it authored or that concerns it, with the seals that prove them.
charter.checked by: the chronicle's replay and archeion's proofs of inclusion

charter.title: Effects outside
charter.text: No operative acts with effect outside the society except under a mandate that names the kind of effect and whose root has legal capacity for it.
charter.checked by: mandates: kinds and matters

charter.title: Receiving capacity
charter.text: Each member declares what it can receive in a round, and contributions beyond it wait or are declined with a reason.
charter.checked by: admission condition 8

charter.title: Notice of incidents
charter.text: A member gives notice to the parties concerned of an incident that touches their records, keys or resources, as an act of a declared kind.
charter.checked by: the chronicle

charter.title: Plural offices
charter.text: Each office of the league is held by more than one party before it is relied on, and a member may use another's office or run its own.
charter.checked by: the custody of means; the report of recognised against executable powers

charter.title: Exit
charter.text: A member leaves with notice of two rounds; commitments made before its exit stay owed.
charter.checked by: the boundary rule; leaving leaves commitments owed

preserved: a member can put a question to the council and have it decided
a person's claim reaches a body that includes a person

captured: the heads of members' chronicles that notaries witness

communities.mission: A conference the forum convenes, at which the communities' envoys decide whether and how to organise a global analysis of the goals.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: Commons proposes a charter. The chair rotates every twelve rounds. The council admits a tool to the bench by a two-thirds vote. Sections receive first review from two peers of other origins. The book is adopted by unanimity. Commons will keep the shelf of data: for each section, series from the World Bank's catalogue are chosen by one gatherer and checked by another of a different origin. Amendmen

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild proposes the following charter: a rotating chair; tools admitted to the bench by two thirds; first review by peers of other origins; the book adopted by unanimity. The guild welcomes amendments from the commons, the cooperative and the forum, particularly on the review stage. One possible amendment is to add a reader from those the goals concern after peer replication.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative proposes a charter with four terms: a standing secretariat, admission of tools to the bench by two thirds, first review of sections by two guild peers of other origins, and adoption of the book by unanimity. The terms are open to amendment by any community.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum proposes a charter that keeps power distributed and puts the people the goals concern at the first reading of every section. It is open to adjusting the thresholds if another community has a concern.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: Commons votes for the identical commons and guild charters: rotating chair, tools admitted by two thirds, peer review, book adopted by unanimity. Commons invites the cooperative to accept a rotating chair, and the forum to accept unanimity for the book, with a reader from those the goals concern added after peer review.

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild supports every charter with peer review of other origins and adoption of the book by unanimity. The commons and guild charters are identical, so convergence on them is near. The guild proposes to the forum that a reading by those the goals concern follow peer replication, as a stage of review rather than the first review.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative accepts a rotating chair and supports the commons and guild charters, which share the same terms. It asks the forum to consent to them, and suggests a later amendment adding a reader from those the goals concern after peer replication, as the guild proposed.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum consents to the commons and guild charter: rotating chair, two thirds for the bench, peers at first review, unanimity for the book. It does so on the understanding, offered by the guild, that a reader from those the goals concern reviews each section after peer replication. Unanimity on the book secures the forum's judgement at the end.

communities.mission: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.

record.author: commons/envoy
record.body: The commons approves the chapters whose sections rest on well-covered World Development Indicators series and the data chapter that records gaps. Several drafted sections (violence against women, food loss, marine pollution, mountain ecosystems, arms transfers) have thin or no WDI coverage; their authors should state the gap, the year range and the unit of whatever proxy is used, and say where a t

record.author: guild/envoy
record.body: The guild supports the draft's breadth. It asks that the data-gaps and interlinkage chapters carry the method and the replication record, so that every stated number, year and unit can be traced to a bench run and an independent replication.

record.author: cooperative/envoy
record.body: The cooperative supports a book in which each number is replicated before it is written. It favours the overview, the core human-development goals, Sub-Saharan Africa, the financing and data chapters, and the proposals, because these carry most of the replicated evidence. It also asks that duplicated financing material in c18 and c27 be coordinated so the two chapters do not repeat each other.

record.author: forum/envoy
record.body: The forum backs the chapters closest to people's lives: poverty, hunger, health, schooling, gender, water, inequality and justice. It also backs the two regions where deprivation concentrates, and the chapters on data gaps and proposals. Its central request is that averages never stand alone. Each chapter should say who is left behind, and where the data cannot say.

record.author: commons/envoy

series.why: Headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), the current international extreme-poverty line, the closest match to the target's measure. It is not the $1.25 line named in the target, so levels and trends are not directly comparable.

Headcount at national poverty lines, the official measures of each country, with wide coverage. It tracks Target 1.2's national definitions, but the lines differ across countries and over time, so cross-country comparison is weak.

Poverty gap at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP), showing how far the poor fall below the line, not just how many they are. It complements the headcount and shares the $3.00 line's mismatch with the $1.25 target.

The nearest available measure is the $3.00 (2021 PPP) headcount, so the section's 2015 and latest-year figures will be for a higher line than the target and will not match the 2015 $1.25 baseline. petition.name: Headcount ratio at $1.25 a day (2011 PPP), SI.POV.1DAY
petition.need: The bench lacks the $1.25 a day headcount that Target 1.1 names. A series at the original 2011 PPP line, back to 1981 or 1990, would allow a like-for-like 2015 baseline and a true test of the 2030 goal.

series.why: Share of population affected by droughts, floods and extreme temperatures; closest to the affected count, but averaged over 1990-2009 and not annual.
New internal displacements linked to disasters, counted as cases; reflects one disaster loss pathway, excludes non-displaced affected people, and is not a headcount.
Disaster risk reduction progress score (1-5), tracking national strategies relevant to target 1.5 exposure and vulnerability; a policy score, not a loss measure.
Poverty headcount at national lines, locating the poor whose resilience target 1.5 addresses; indicates who is vulnerable, not losses from shocks.

d-c02-5~loom/gatherer~16.note: The catalogue holds no annual count of people affected by disasters and no direct loss series, so the figures above are partial. EN.CLC.MDAT.ZS is a 1990-2009 average, not a current figure, and must be reported as such. Target 1.5 can be read as a resilience aim (reducing vulnerability) or as an exp

petition.name: Disaster loss and affected-population series
petition.need: Annual series for deaths from disasters (SDG 1.5.1), direct economic losses as a share of GDP (SDG 1.5.2), and people affected by disasters per year, with units and years stated, so the section can report current losses rather than 1990-2009 averages.

series.why: Headcount at national poverty lines, % of population; the direct measure of Target 1.2 under national definitions. Limits: national lines differ across countries, and survey years are irregular and sparse.
Headcount at the societal poverty line, % of population; a cross-country benchmark of living standards that complements national lines. Limits: modelled from few surveys, with gaps in coverage.

World Bank multidimensional poverty headcount, % of population; captures poverty in several dimensions, as Target 1.2 requires. Limits: sparse survey years, with recent data missing for many countries.

UNDP and OPHI multidimensional poverty headcount, % of population; a second multidimensional measure for cross-checking the World Bank series. Limits: derived from household surveys with irregular timing.

d-c02-2~cedar/gatherer~16.note: The national-line series (SI.POV.NAHC) is the core indicator for Target 1.2, but its data are irregular and differ in definition across countries, so headcounts over 2015 to 2030 cannot be compared directly without noting the line used. Multidimensional series approximate the target's words 'in all

petition.name: Coverage and recency indicator for national poverty lines
petition.need: A series giving, for each year from 2015, the number of countries with a national-line poverty estimate and the survey year used, so that missing data and a target read in more than one way (national lines versus multidimensional measures) can be reported exactly.

series.why: Not listed in candidates; closest is coverage of safety nets in poorest quintile, but code absent, so choose listed equivalent below.
Coverage of all social protection and labour programmes as % of population; measures the target's concern with substantial coverage, though not restricted to the poorest quintile.
Share of total SPL benefits reaching the poorest quintile; directly answers how far programmes favour the poorest, though it is a share of benefits, not coverage of the poor.
Safety-net coverage of the poorest quintile as % of population; the closest match to the question, but it is a sub-programme measure, not all programmes.
Social insurance coverage of the poorest quintile as % of population; shows contributory reach among the poor, which is typically low, with limits from survey definitions.

d-c02-3~quarry/gatherer~16.note: The question asks for the share of the poorest quintile covered by social protection and labour programmes. The catalogue offers no series for all-programme coverage within the poorest quintile; the nearest listed items are benefit incidence and sub-programme coverage. Per_sa_allsa.cov_q1_tot is lis

petition.name: All-programme coverage for the poorest quintile
petition.need: A series giving coverage of all social protection and labour programmes (per_allsp) for the poorest quintile, measured as % of population in that quintile, so that the question is answered directly rather than through safety-net or insurance subsets.

series.why: Aggregate official development assistance received by developing countries, the inflow target 1.a describes. Current dollars, so inflation distorts; not poverty-specific.
Total net bilateral aid from DAC donors, showing donor effort. Bilateral channels only, excluding multilateral flows; current dollars; not poverty-targeted.
Share of social protection and labour benefits reaching the poorest fifth, directly measuring the pro-poor spending that target 1.b addresses. Survey-based, with country gaps.
Government education spending as share of total government spending, a proxy for priority to essential services. Education only; recent years often missing.
Domestic government health spending as share of general government spending, a proxy for essential service priority. Health only; excludes household out-of-pocket payments.

d-c02-6~bao/gatherer~16.note: No candidate measures total government spending on essential services or aid specifically for poverty reduction; the chosen series are proxies. Targets 1.a and 1.b admit more than one reading of adequate means and pro-poor spending, and the figures should be read with that in mind.

petition.name: Government spending on social protection, percentage of GDP, and poverty-coded official aid
petition.need: The bench lacks a series for total government expenditure on social protection as a share of GDP, and for aid tagged to poverty reduction. Either would measure targets 1.a and 1.b directly.

verdicts.why: Current international extreme-poverty headcount and the closest match to Target 1.1; the $3.00 line differs from the $1.25 target, a mismatch the section must state.
National lines vary by country and year, so they cannot answer the international-line question and weaken cross-country comparison.
Poverty gap shows depth as well as incidence, which supports the section's claim that extreme poverty misses zero.

petition.name: World Bank Poverty and Inequality Platform, headcount at the $1.25 a day line (2011 PPP)
petition.need: The target names the $1.25 line, which the chosen series does not report; the legacy $1.25 series is needed for 2015 and the latest year, or a note that it is discontinued.

series.why: Share of population using at least basic drinking water services; measures target 1.4 access to basic services, wide coverage, but 'basic' is a lower bar than safely managed.
Share of population using at least basic sanitation services; directly tracks basic sanitation access named in target 1.4, though it hides quality and sharing of facilities.
Share of population with access to electricity; a core basic-service measure under target 1.4, with wide coverage, though access does not imply reliability or affordability.
Rural basic drinking water share, exposing the urban-rural gap that the question about the poor requires; known limit is that rural populations are where the poor concentrate.
Rural electricity access share, showing where the poor lack power; it does not separate income groups, so the poor's position must be inferred from location.

d-c02-4~cedar/gatherer~20.note: The catalogue offers no income-quintile breakdown of water, sanitation or electricity access, so the poor cannot be identified directly; rural and urban splits serve as proxies, and this proxy limit should be stated in the text. Safely managed series (SH.H2O.SMDW, SH.STA.SMSS) measure a stricter sta

petition.name: Bench request for income-quintile access series
petition.need: A World Development Indicators series giving water, sanitation and electricity access by wealth quintile, so the section can measure the poor's access directly rather than through rural and urban proxies.

verdicts.why: Only affected-population share for disasters in the set; answers the affected question, but its 1990-2009 average is dated and not annual.
Counts new disaster-linked displacement cases, one real loss pathway. Cases are not people, and non-displaced affected people are excluded, so say so.
A self-assessed policy score from 2009-2011 reports, not a measure of people affected or losses incurred.
Locates the poor whose resilience target 1.5 addresses, as context only; it does not measure losses from shocks.

add.why: Records economic loss from outages, a shock-driven loss to firms; it is not disaster-specific, so the section must say so.

verdicts.why: Safety-net coverage of the poorest quintile is the closest match to the question. It is listed twice; keep one copy.
All-programme coverage as % of population tests substantial coverage, though it is not restricted to the poorest quintile.
Share of benefits reaching the poorest quintile, not coverage of the poor; useful as a targeting complement with that caveat.
Social insurance coverage of the poorest quintile shows contributory reach among the poor, which survey definitions may limit.

add.why: Income share of the lowest 20% gives context for the poorest quintile that the coverage series lack.
Share of safety-net benefits reaching the poorest quintile complements coverage by showing targeting of the poor.

verdicts.why: Headcount at national poverty lines is the direct measure of Target 1.2 under national definitions.
The societal line is a cross-country benchmark, not a national definition, so it does not measure Target 1.2 as worded.
Multidimensional headcount covers several dimensions, as Target 1.2 requires; sparse recent data must be flagged.
A second multidimensional measure allows cross-checking the World Bank series; coverage is thinner and must be noted.

add.why: The $3.00 international headcount offers the contrast the section needs between national and international lines.
The poverty gap shows depth of poverty, which headcounts alone do not reveal when asking how poverty changed.

verdicts.why: Aggregate net ODA received directly measures the inflow that target 1.a describes. Current dollars need deflating, and it is not poverty-specific.
Largely a subset of the aggregate ODA series already kept, and it covers only bilateral channels, which the section does not need.
Share of social protection benefits reaching the poorest fifth directly measures pro-poor spending for target 1.b. Survey-based, with country gaps.
Education's share of government spending proxies priority for essential services. It covers education only, and recent years are often missing.
Domestic government health share of public spending proxies essential-service priority. It excludes household out-of-pocket payments, so note that gap.

add.why: Share facing impoverishing out-of-pocket health spending shows whether essential services protect households from poverty, which the spending series alone cannot show.
Adequacy of benefits as a share of beneficiary welfare shows whether pro-poor transfers are large enough to matter, complementing the incidence series.

verdicts.why: National share using at least basic drinking water; the broadest target 1.4 access measure, though 'basic' is a lower bar than safely managed.
National share using at least basic sanitation; tracks the sanitation access named in target 1.4, but hides quality and shared facilities.
National share with electricity access; a core basic-service measure, though access does not imply reliability or affordability.
Rural basic water share exposes the urban-rural gap; it does not measure the poor directly, so their position is inferred from location.
Rural electricity share shows where power is lacking; it does not separate income groups, so the poor's position is inferred from location.

add.why: Rural basic sanitation share is missing from the set, leaving the rural sanitation gap unmeasured while rural water is tracked.
Urban basic water share is needed beside the rural series to show the full urban-rural gap in water access.

plan.why: Gives the share below $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) for the world, seven regions and four income groups in 2015 and the latest year, with the countries reporting; this answers the question directly.
Survey data are sparse and lagged, so the number of countries reporting each year shows how firm the 2015 and latest-year figures are, and where data are missing.

params.target_reading: Target 1.1 says 'eradicate extreme poverty', read as a headcount near zero by 2030; the text cites $1.25 a day, but the series uses $3.00 (2021 PPP), so the line differs and a zero-share reading is an interpretation (a 3 per cent threshold is used elsewhere).

plan.why: Compares the compound rate of decline since 2015 with the rate needed to reach zero by 2030, showing whether the world and regions are on course.

params.target_reading: Same reading as above: eradication taken as zero share in 2030.

plan.why: Counts countries in each progress class, showing how many are on track, slow or reversing.
Shows whether poverty is concentrating in fewer countries and how much of the inequality lies between regions.

w-c02-2-1~loom/writer-1~44.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and 15 did in 2001. The number rose to 22 in 2002 and 21 in 2003, then to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005.

Across the years 2006 to 2008 the count held at 40 each year. It reached 47 in 2009 and 50 in 2010, then stood at 49 in 2011 and 50 in 2012. It fell to 45 in 2013 and 46 in 2014. In 2015, the baseline year of the goals, 55 countries reported, followed by 57 in 2016 and 53 in 2017. The peak came later: 67 in 2018, 62 in 2019, 57 in 2020 and 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much. The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008 and 33 in 2009, then jumped to 69 in 2010. It stood at 61 in 2011, 71 in 2012, 61 in 2013 and 69 in 2014.

The count reached 74 in 2015, 72 in 2016 and 67 in 2017, with a high of 84 in 2018. It then fell to 71 in 2019, 58 in 2020, 69 in 2021 and 63 in 2022. The last years are sparse: 48 countries in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. The multidimensional series is somewhat better populated than the national-line series in the middle years, but both lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. The classification should be read with that ambiguity in mind: a national line is set by each country, and it may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

The split is therefore not even. Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, which shows that large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. The population shares describe only the countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.649 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line as well.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other. The national and international lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of 0.025885 with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The coefficient is positive. Given the setup of the test, this does not indicate that countries with higher starting headcounts fell faster. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence rather than catching up.

### Proposals

The findings lead to the proposals listed below.

proposals: Statistical offices and their funders should prioritise the timely publication of national-line headcounts, so that the 2023 to 2025 reporting counts of 40, 31 and 13 countries are filled in before the 2030 assessment.
Countries should publish the national poverty line in force for each survey year and flag any revision, so that changes in definition can be separated from changes in poverty.
Monitoring bodies should report national-line and international-line results side by side, since the two move together in level but only loosely in change.
Attention and support should be directed to the 34 countries in regression, and to the widening spread among the 25 countries in the convergence sample.

Coverage of recent years is thin, and the trend classes rest on 94 countries only. National lines differ in definition and may be revised, and no numeric halving target is set in the assessment. The comparison with the $3.00 line covers 21 countries and the convergence test 25. Poverty in all its dimensions by national definitions, including by sex and age, is not covered here.

w-c02-3-1~cedar/writer-1~44.text:
### What the coverage record contains

Target 1.3 asks for nationally appropriate social protection systems, including floors, and for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The question put to the data is what share of the poorest quintile is reached by social protection and labour programmes. The bench's tools answer only part of it. They hold the coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population, but the results available here describe how many countries report and how unequal the reported coverage is. They do not give a level for the world or for any region. No world or regional aggregate exists for this indicator, so no global coverage figure is stated in this section.

The reporting record is thin. Across the whole series, 121 countries have reported in at least one year. In any single year far fewer have done so. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2003 the figure was 2 again. The count rose to 11 in 2005, 22 in 2007 and 35 in 2009. It reached 41 in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013, recovered to 35 in 2014 and stood at 38 in 2015.

### Reporting peaks in 2018 and then collapses

The highest annual count is 47 countries in 2018. After that the record shrinks: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reports for 2023. The same single country appears in the companion series on social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, which also has 1 country reporting in 2023.

Two cautions follow. First, the fall after 2018 is partly a matter of survey timing and publication lag, so the recent years are incomplete and should not be read as a decline in coverage. Second, the set of reporting countries changes from year to year, so movements in the count are not movements in the world. A comparison between years mixes changes in coverage with changes in who is measured. The 2030 deadline falls in a period when the most recent observations are the scarcest.

### Coverage is becoming more even among reporting countries

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, narrows across the three years examined. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157 and the Theil 0.1668. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056 and the Theil 0.0942. The coefficient of variation moved from 0.5784 in 2015 to 0.5577 in 2018 and 0.3912 in 2021.

The decomposition changes character as well. In 2015, regional differences accounted for 0.7408 of the Theil index, so most of the inequality lay between regions. By 2018 that share was 0.2878, and by 2021 it was 0.2137. Differences within regions therefore dominate in the later years. This does not show that the poorest quintile is well covered. A narrowing spread is compatible with uniformly low coverage, and it may reflect a different group of countries in each year, since the sample falls from 47 to 30 between 2018 and 2021. The figures for the spread and the single-country social insurance series are shown in figures c02-3.r2 and c02-3.r3.

### Reading the target

The wording of target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a threshold, and the indicator measures participation in programmes, not the adequacy of benefits or whether the floor is reached in practice. The safety net series and the social insurance series measure different things, and neither captures informal or community support. The data therefore cannot establish whether the target is on track.

claims.fact: c02-3.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Statistical agencies and funders should treat household survey frequency as a core part of target 1.3, so that each country reports poorest-quintile coverage at least once every three years.
Reporting should publish the list of countries behind each annual figure and any aggregate, so that changes in the sample are not mistaken for changes in coverage.
Programme coverage should be paired with data on benefit adequacy, so that the target can be judged on whether the floor protects the poor and not on participation alone.
w-c02-3-1~cedar/writer-1~44.gaps: The results give no level of coverage for the poorest quintile, no world or regional aggregate, and no country-by-country values in the text. Reporting is sparse and shifting, and 2023 has a single country. Benefit adequacy, informal support, the vulnerable beyond the poorest quintile, and the meaning of substantial coverage are not covered.

w-c02-4-1~cedar/writer-2~44.text:
Access to basic services is the plainest test of target 1.4, which asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated, and they are drawn from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. They measure coverage of the population, not the income of those covered, so they show where service gaps lie and not directly who among the poor is excluded.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. The regional spread is wide. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to reach 59.4914% in 2030, which leaves roughly four in ten rural residents without basic water even if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water everywhere

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population share. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access is closing the gap but not in Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain in annual rate yet still the lowest level. Its projected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed, and Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, resting on the regional pattern above and on the limits of national averages.

claims.fact: c02-4.r4: countries on track or target met
c02-4.r4: population share on track or target met
c02-4.r4: countries moderate progress, but acceleration needed
c02-4.r4: countries marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed
c02-4.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-4.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2024

proposals: Direct concessional finance and technical support to rural sanitation in Sub-Saharan Africa, where coverage is lowest and gains are slowest.
Pair rural electrification programmes in Sub-Saharan Africa with water and sanitation investment, so that connection to one service helps the others.
Monitor the 39 countries where sanitation coverage is regressing and report the causes publicly, with conflict, population growth and data revision considered.
Report service access by income quintile and by sex of household head, so that target 1.4 can be tracked for the poor directly.
w-c02-4-1~cedar/writer-2~44.gaps: The indicators are rural averages and do not break coverage down by income, sex, disability or informal settlement, so the poor are not identified directly. Basic service levels exclude quality, reliability and affordability. Country reporting varies by year and indicator, and the trend classes depend on a linear reading of 100% by 2030, which can be read differently for countries already near the ceiling. Access to land, property, inheritance and financial services, also named in target 1.4, is not covered here.

w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-3~44.text:
### Displacement from disasters has grown

The data available to the cooperative measure disaster impact through one indicator: new internal displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. Globally the count rose from 19188817 in 2015 to 26393278 in 2023. The indicator records displacement, not deaths, injuries or economic damage. Monetary losses are therefore not covered here, and the question of losses is answered only in so far as displacement is a loss of home and livelihood.

The figure is a count of cases, not of distinct people, so one person displaced twice may appear twice. The World Bank series draws on reports of displacement events, and the figures should be read as the best available record rather than a census.

### Regions diverge sharply

East Asia and Pacific remained the largest regional contributor in both years, with 8304660 cases in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023. South Asia moved the other way, falling from 6877900 in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. A fall of that size may reflect fewer events, better early warning and evacuation practice, or differences in reporting; the data do not distinguish among these.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest growth among the large regions, from 1108287 in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; the series begins in 2016 for this region, so the comparison starts a year later than the others. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping roughly doubled, from 1212730 to 2481660. Latin America and the Caribbean changed modestly, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000, a small base in absolute terms.

### Concentration has increased

Among countries, weighted by population, inequality in displacement grew between the two years. The Gini coefficient rose from 0.5701 in 2015 to 0.6783 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.7232 to 0.8935. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.1066 to 1.4691. Displacement is therefore more unevenly distributed across countries in 2023 than in 2015.

The share of that inequality lying between regions fell from 0.7075 to 0.5301. Differences within regions now account for a larger part of the spread, so regional averages hide more than they did. A regional response alone would miss the countries bearing the heaviest burden.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting rose from 80 in 2008 to 145 in 2023, with 199 economies reporting in at least one year. Coverage dipped to 60 in 2009 and 62 in 2011, then reached 118 in 2013 and 112 in 2015. The 2015 spread analysis covers 112 countries and the 2023 analysis 145. Part of the global rise may thus reflect wider reporting rather than more displacement. The 2015 to 2023 comparison is better founded than comparisons with earlier years, but it is not like for like.

Target 1.5 can also be read in more than one way: it speaks of reducing exposure and vulnerability, while this indicator measures an outcome of hazards. A rise in displacement does not alone show greater vulnerability, since larger populations in exposed areas, more events or better counting could each contribute.

claims.fact: c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Disaster displacement should be tracked alongside poverty measures in national reporting, so that resilience under Target 1.5 is judged by outcomes as well as by plans.
Support for early warning and evacuation should be directed first to the countries with the largest displacement, since within-region differences now explain more of the spread.
Statistical offices should be funded to report displacement consistently every year, so that rises driven by better counting can be separated from rises in events.
Monetary loss, mortality and displacement should be reported together in a common series, so the full cost of disasters to poor households can be seen.
w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-3~44.gaps: The data do not cover deaths, injuries, damage to homes and assets, or economic losses in money terms, nor the income of those displaced or how long displacement lasts. Cases are not distinct people. Reporting coverage changed over time, so earlier years are not comparable. No data link displacement to poverty status or to climate causes.

petition.need: A World Bank series on economic losses and deaths from disasters, by country and year, to complement the displacement counts.

w-c02-1-1~rowan/writer-1~44.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030. The target text quoted in the framework refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices, expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a higher, revised line than the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which the trend tool uses as its goal.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. Projected along its own 2015 to 2024 path, the world ratio would reach 8.365 per cent in 2030. The trend tool rates this as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and gives a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.376. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration. North America starts from a low level, so the slow pace there reflects a small remaining headcount more than a large one.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of four years, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions with nine years of data.

Two regions fall short in a different way. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved the wrong way, from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent, a ratio of -0.481 and a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa and this group are therefore where the world's gap to zero is widest and growing least tractable.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent. Nearly a quarter of assessed countries are therefore moving away from the target, and the share of population in regression is larger than that in stagnation and marginal progress combined only in part: 17.88 per cent against 13.45 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each period is slower than the one before. At the latest pace, the remaining 10.1 per cent would not reach zero by 2030.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean. Poverty is becoming more concentrated in fewer places rather than evenly shrinking.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. Reporting then ranged between 70 and 93 countries a year to 2022, with 93 in 2018, and fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values are thus largely estimated or modelled from a small number of recent surveys, and no regional values are given for 2025. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 are made with that caution.

### Proposals

The proposals that follow from these findings are addressed to the actors named in each.

Only 26 countries reported in 2024 and 4 in 2025, so recent values are thinly supported. South Asia has data only from 2020. The data give no breakdown by sex, age or location, and say nothing of depth of poverty or of people just above the line. Projections extend past trends and do not model shocks.

w-c02-6-1~dahlia/writer-1~47.text:
### Education spending has slipped as a share of budgets

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, shows little movement at the global level and a drift downward in most regions. The world figure was 14.1095% in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The small global change conceals larger regional shifts. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022, and Europe & Central Asia from 11.8212% in 2015 to 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares have also lost ground, with one exception. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it says nothing about whether spending reaches the poorest households. The end years also differ by region, so the comparisons are not over identical periods. For 2025, only 60 countries report, so the latest South Asian figure rests on thin coverage.

### Health spending is lowest where need is greatest

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, differs widely between regions. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it improved from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the series ends there in the regional view, so later change cannot be judged. The gap between North America and South Asia in the latest years shown is large, and the rise in South Asia leaves it well short of every other region listed.

Coverage of this indicator is good until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year with broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only: Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia & Pacific and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent from the regional figures.

### Aid has grown, and most of it goes to a few regions

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan saw the steepest increase, from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493 over the same years.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America's series is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, and is not a meaningful comparator. These figures are in current dollars, so part of the growth reflects prices, and the series does not distinguish aid aimed at poverty reduction from aid for other purposes. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend therefore cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. Spending shares and aid totals can show direction and scale. They cannot show whether the money reached people in poverty.

### Proposals

The evidence supports several proposals, set out below.

claims.fact: c02-6.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2016
c02-6.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2022
c02-6.r5: countries reporting in any year
c02-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2021
c02-6.r4: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Countries and statistical agencies should report the share of budgets spent on education and health alongside spending per person, so that falling shares can be told apart from falling real resources.
Donors should publish aid by purpose, separating poverty-reduction spending from other aid, so that growth in totals can be tied to Target 1.a.
South Asia's health spending share, still far below other regions, should be a priority for domestic budget reform and targeted support.
Statistical agencies should fund regular household surveys so that benefit incidence for the poorest fifth is reported by many more countries each year.
w-c02-6-1~dahlia/writer-1~47.gaps: The data do not show spending per person, real-terms changes, or whether spending reached poor households. Aid is not split by purpose or by least developed country status, and the regional aid series end in 2021. Health aggregates are missing for two regions, and latest-year coverage is thin for education in 2025 and health in 2024. Benefit incidence for the poorest fifth has no aggregates and erratic country coverage. Gender-sensitive policy under Target 1.b is not measured by any series used here.

w-c02-3-1~cedar/writer-1~48.text:
The question for this section is what share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot yet answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile. No regional or world aggregate is available for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

Coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, measured as a percentage of that quintile, rests on household surveys. Survey timing therefore sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000 two countries reported, and in 2002 three. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013, a drop that reflects survey cycles rather than any change in policy. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count declined: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only one country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The figure shows that the indicator has some historical reach, but in any single year fewer than half of those countries are observed. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion narrows as the sample shrinks

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was measured for three years. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini fell to 0.2056, the Theil index to 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation to 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality changes sharply

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a larger shift. In 2015, regional differences accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index, expressed in the data as 0.7408. By 2018 the between-region share was 0.2878, and by 2021 it was 0.2137. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. By 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region.

The change is large enough to suggest that the composition of the sample, not only the policies of governments, drives the result. Regions represented by few countries in 2015 may have been better represented later, which would shift the weight from the between-region to the within-region component. The data given here do not allow that explanation to be tested.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only one country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world. Social insurance, which includes contributory pensions and unemployment benefits, is the kind of protection that often misses people in informal work, but the data here cannot show whether that is so.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding for this section is therefore about the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse, irregular and declining in recent reporting.

claims.fact: c02-3.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Governments and statistical offices should field the household surveys that measure social protection coverage on a regular cycle, so that at least the countries reporting in 2018 report again in each later survey round.

The World Bank and partner agencies should publish regional and world aggregates for coverage in the poorest quintile, with the sample of countries stated, so that progress on target 1.3 can be read at all.
The custodians of the indicator framework should define substantial coverage as a numerical threshold for the poorest quintile, so that reported figures can be judged against it.
w-c02-3-1~cedar/writer-1~48.gaps: The data give no global or regional level of coverage for the poorest quintile, only the number of reporting countries and the spread among them. The samples differ between years, so trends cannot be separated from changes in who is observed. Social insurance coverage is observed for one country in 2023. The data do not capture the adequacy or quality of benefits, informal or non-survey support, or protection for the vulnerable beyond the poorest fifth. Target 1.3 does not define substantial coverage numerically.

w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-3~48.text:
### Displacement from disasters has risen

Target 1.5 asks that the poor and those in vulnerable situations be made more resilient to climate-related extreme events and other shocks by 2030. The indicator available through the World Development Indicators is new internal displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. It measures people forced to move, not the economic losses that followed. The question of losses can therefore be answered only in part.

Worldwide, new displacement associated with disasters rose from 19188817 cases in 2015 to 26393278 cases in 2023. Because the unit is cases, a person displaced twice in a year may be counted twice, and the figure is not a count of distinct people. The rise is substantial, yet two years do not make a trend, and disaster years vary widely. The figure for 2023 shows one year, not a decade.

### Regional patterns diverge

The regional record is uneven. East Asia & Pacific remains the largest region, moving from 8304660 cases in 2015 to 9038561 in 2023. South Asia is the one region with a fall, from 6877900 in 2015 to 2446054 in 2023. Whether that fall reflects better preparedness, milder seasons or changes in reporting cannot be settled from these data.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the sharpest rise among the large regions, from 1108287 cases in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Europe & Central Asia rose from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023, the series beginning in 2016 because no 2015 value is given. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from 1212730 to 2481660. Latin America & Caribbean changed little, from 1543360 to 1728025. North America rose from 76000 to 394000, a small base.

### Concentration and coverage limit the reading

Displacement has become more concentrated among countries. Weighted by population, the Gini coefficient of the indicator rose from 0.570 in 2015 to 0.678 in 2023, and the Theil index from 0.723 to 0.893. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8 per cent in 2015 to 53.0 per cent in 2023. Differences within regions therefore matter more than before, and regional averages hide them. The two years also differ in country count, 112 in 2015 and 145 in 2023, so part of the change in spread may come from wider reporting.

Coverage has itself changed. The number of countries reporting was 80 in 2008, fell to 60 in 2009, and reached 118 in 2013. It stood at 112 in 2015, 141 in 2018 and 144 in 2022, before reaching 145 in 2023. In all, 199 economies have reported in at least one year. Part of the apparent rise in global displacement may thus reflect more complete counting, particularly in earlier years, though the 2015 to 2023 comparison rests on a far fuller base than the years before 2013.

### Proposals

The findings support the proposals below.

claims.fact: c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: National statistical offices should report disaster displacement with a common definition and publish economic losses alongside it, so that Target 1.5 can be monitored on both people and assets.
Governments in Sub-Saharan Africa and Europe & Central Asia, where displacement has risen most, should prioritise early warning and shelter planning for poor households.
Reporting countries should flag repeat displacement of the same people, so that cases can be separated from individuals.
Donors should study what lowered displacement in South Asia and finance the transfer of those practices to other regions.
w-c02-5-1~cedar/writer-3~48.gaps: The data give new displacement cases only. They do not cover deaths, people affected in other ways, economic losses, damage to homes or crops, or the share of those displaced who are poor. Cases may count one person more than once. Coverage was thin before 2013, and the 2015 and 2023 country sets differ. The data do not attribute displacement to climate change, and Target 1.5 can be read as covering shocks beyond disasters.

petition.name: Disaster loss data
petition.need: Series on economic losses and people affected by disasters, by country and year, disaggregated by income, to measure Target 1.5 fully.

t-national-poverty-line-metadata~orchard.name: national-poverty-line-metadata
t-national-poverty-line-metadata~orchard.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    gap = params.get('jump_threshold', 5.0)
    country = params.get('country')
    s = data[code]
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    flagged = []
    counted = 0
    obs_total = 0
    for unit in s:
        series = s[unit]
        if unit not in regions:
            continue
        if country is not None and unit != country:
            continue
        years = sorted(series.keys())
        if len(years) == 0:
            continue
        counted += 1
        obs_total += len(years)
        for i in range(1, len(years)):
            a = series[years[i-1]]
            b = series[years[i]]
            d = b - a
            if abs(d) >= gap:
                flagged.append((abs(d), unit, years[i-1], years[i], d))
    flagged.sort(reverse=True)
    top = flagged[:5]
    facts = {'countries_with_data': counted, 'observations': obs_total, 'jumps_flagged': len(flagged), 'threshold': gap}
    if top:
        t = top[0]
        facts['largest_jump_country'] = names.get(t[1], t[1])
        facts['largest_jump_from_year'] = t[2]
        facts['largest_jump_to_year'] = t[3]
        facts['largest_jump_value'] = round(t[4], 2)
    parts = []
    for t in top:
        parts.append(names.get(t[1], t[1]) + ' ' + str(t[2]) + ' to ' + str(t[3]) + ': ' + str(round(t[4], 2)))
    summary = 'Between consecutive survey years, ' + str(len(flagged)) + ' changes of at least ' + str(gap) + ' were found across ' + str(counted) + ' countries (' + str(obs_total) + ' observations). The data carry no poverty-line metadata, so a jump marks a candidate definitional revision to check against national sources, not a confirmed one. '
    if parts:
        summary += 'Largest: ' + '; '.join(parts) + '.'
    else:
        summary += 'No jumps at this threshold.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}
t-national-poverty-line-metadata~orchard.about: Screens a series for large changes between consecutive survey years per country, to flag candidate definitional breaks (such as poverty-line revisions) for follow-up. The World Bank data supply no line metadata, so flags are candidates only.

params.series: Series code to screen, which must also appear in series_params
params.jump_threshold: Smallest absolute change between consecutive observed years to flag, in the series unit; default 5.0
params.country: Optional country code to restrict the screen to one country

w-c02-5-1~loom/writer-1~52.text:
### Displacement from disasters has risen

The indicator available to the cooperative for Target 1.5 is new internal displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. Worldwide it stood at 19188817 in 2015 and reached 26393278 in 2023. The measure counts displacement events, not distinct people, so one person displaced twice appears twice. It also says nothing about economic loss. No figure for damage, lost income or lost assets was retrieved, so the question of what losses followed can be answered only through displacement.

The rise is not uniform. East Asia & Pacific recorded 8304660 in 2015 and 9038561 in 2023, a modest increase from a high base. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 1543360 to 1728025 over the same years. South Asia fell from 6877900 to 2446054, the only region in the series with a large decline. Such a fall may reflect fewer severe events in a given year, better early warning or changes in reporting, and the data cannot separate these explanations.

### Growth is steepest where capacity is thinnest

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1108287 in 2015 to 6029739 in 2023. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from 1212730 to 2481660. Europe & Central Asia rose from 56782 in 2016 to 4275239 in 2023; its series begins a year later than the others, and the starting value is small enough that the change may owe much to improved counting. North America rose from 76000 to 394000. Because each of these regions started from a lower level than East Asia & Pacific, their shares of the world total shifted markedly between the two years.

Annual totals are dominated by single large events, so two end-years cannot establish a trend. The comparison between 2015 and 2023 should be read as two observations, not as a smooth path.

### Reporting has widened, which complicates comparison

The number of countries reporting was 80 in 2008 and 60 in 2009, then 118 in 2013, 112 in 2015 and 145 in 2023. In all, 199 countries reported in at least one year. Part of the rise in the world total may therefore reflect more complete counting; the 2015 figure rests on 112 countries and the 2023 figure on 145. The coverage dip in 2021, at 133 countries, against 142 in 2020, shows that coverage is not rising steadily.

### Unevenness among countries has increased

Population-weighted, the Gini coefficient of displacement across countries was 0.570 in 2015, with 112 countries, and 0.678 in 2023, with 145. The Theil index rose from 0.723 to 0.893. The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 70.8% to 53.0%, so a growing part of the inequality lies between countries within the same region. Displacement has become more concentrated in a few countries, and regional averages hide this. These measures describe how unequal the burden is across countries; they do not say whether the poor within each country are those displaced.

claims.fact: c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Report disaster displacement alongside economic loss and loss of assets for the same events, so that Target 1.5 can be judged on both people and value.
Publish displacement counts with a note on how many distinct people they cover, so that repeat displacement is visible.
Direct resilience finance to the countries where displacement is concentrated, using country data and not regional averages.
Support national statistical offices that do not yet report, so that a stable country panel allows trends to be separated from changes in coverage.
w-c02-5-1~loom/writer-1~52.gaps: The data give displacement cases only. They give no economic loss, no deaths, no count of people affected by type of disaster and no link to household poverty status. Counts are of events, not distinct people, and coverage changed from 112 to 145 countries between 2015 and 2023. Targets 1.5 can be read as exposure, vulnerability or loss, and this indicator measures only one of these.

petition.name: disaster loss and affected-population series
petition.need: Data on economic loss, deaths and people affected by disasters, by country and year, with household poverty status, are needed to answer the question fully.

w-c02-2-2~cedar/writer-1~52.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much.

The indicator has no aggregate series. No global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it, so the data given here do not support a statement of how the headcount changed worldwide. Change can be described only country by country, as in the next section.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025.

Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. It is better populated in most middle years, but both series lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions. Shares below are given to one decimal place.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 regresses each country's change in headcount on its starting level. A negative coefficient would mean that countries starting higher fell faster. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The positive sign means that higher starting headcounts were associated with larger increases or smaller falls, not catching up.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence, though the group is small and may not represent all countries.

### Proposals

The proposals below follow from the coverage gaps and the divergence found above.
