w-c02-6-4~dahlia/writer-1~71.text:
### Education shares fell in most regions

The question put to this section is how much governments spend on essential services and how much aid supports poverty reduction. Essential services are covered here by two budget shares only, education and health. No series available to the bench separates aid aimed at poverty reduction from other aid, so no figure for pro-poor aid exists in these data.

Government expenditure on education, as a share of total government expenditure, was 14.1095% for the world in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The global change is small, but five of the seven regions fell. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa fell from 16.9629% in 2015 to 15.3772% in 2024, a large drop from the highest starting share. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Europe & Central Asia was nearly flat, at 11.8212% in 2015 and 11.685% in 2022, and Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024.

End years differ from 2022 to 2025, and one region starts in 2016, so the spans are not identical and comparisons between regions are indicative only. The count of 60 countries reporting in 2025 belongs to the education series as a whole, not to South Asia alone; it shows that the most recent endpoints rest on a thin base. A budget share is not an amount per child and does not show whether spending reaches the poorest households.

### Health spending shares differ widely between regions

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, varies strongly by region. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it rose from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the regional series ends there, so later change cannot be judged. The data give no measure of need, so they show the gap in budget share but not whether the low South Asian share is too low relative to need.

Country coverage is broad until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year of broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only; East Asia & Pacific and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent.

### Aid rose in every region with a 2015 to 2021 series

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world, in current dollars. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rose from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493. The rise for that region is about 81 per cent and for Sub-Saharan Africa about 39 per cent; both percentages are calculated by the cooperative from the figures given and are not reported facts. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region therefore had the largest proportional rise.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America has no 2015 to 2021 series and is left out of this comparison; its only recorded values are trivial, US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004.

Because the figures are in current dollars, part of the growth reflects prices. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. They show direction and scale, not whether money reached people in poverty.

### Proposals

First, aid reporting should flag the share of aid directed to poverty reduction, so that Target 1.a can be assessed. Second, aid should be published in constant prices alongside current dollars. Third, education and health spending should be reported per child and per person as well as by budget share. Fourth, countries should report the benefit incidence of social protection to the poorest fifth every year, so that a trend can be built.

w-c02-5-3~cedar/writer-1~72.text:
### Displacement counts answer only part of the question

The question asks how many people were affected by disasters and what losses followed. The World Development Indicators supply one series that bears on it: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. No answer on losses is possible from this series, because it records no monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods. It also counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income and cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Target 1.5 asks for the resilience of the poor and of those in vulnerable situations to be built and for their exposure to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced; this series speaks only to exposure, and only in the form of displacement cases.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because displacement depends heavily on the severity of the events in a given year. The comparison is also affected by reporting coverage, discussed below, so the rise is reported with that caveat and is not a firm finding of worsening exposure.

### Regional movements diverge

East Asia and Pacific recorded 8,304,660 cases in 2015 and 9,038,561 cases in 2023, the highest regional figures in both years. South Asia moved the other way, from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 cases in 2023. A fall of this size may reflect the particular events of the two years rather than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions, from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023; the starting year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1,212,730 cases in 2015 to 2,481,660 cases in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 cases to 1,728,025 cases. North America rose from 76,000 cases to 394,000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These counts show where displacing events grew, not who was displaced. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the people affected.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting has changed considerably. In 2008 it was 80 and in 2009 it was 60. It then rose to 118 in 2013, fell to 99 in 2014 and stood at 112 in 2015. It reached 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, dipped to 133 in 2021, and was 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once.

Some of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may therefore come from wider reporting, since 112 countries reported in 2015 and 145 in 2023. The global figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

### Spread among countries widened in the reported sample

Among reporting countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.5701 in 2015 and 0.6783 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.7232 to 0.8935 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: within the reporting sample, displacement is spread more unevenly in 2023 than in 2015. Because the sample grew from 112 countries to 145, part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The share of the Theil index lying between regions fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. In 2015 most of the unevenness came from differences between regions; by 2023 a larger share came from differences among countries within regions. A response designed only by region would therefore miss a growing part of the unevenness, though the sample change makes this a cautious reading.

proposals: National statistical offices should report disaster losses, deaths and damage to livelihoods alongside displacement cases, so that the question of losses can be answered.
Displacement should be reported with income or poverty breakdowns, so that the exposure of the poor can be measured directly.
Planning for disaster resilience should combine regional and national measures, treating the widening spread as provisional until reporting coverage is stable.

Only two end years are compared, and annual event severity is not separated from trend.

t-country-level-national-line-headcount-.name: country-level-national-line-headcount-se
t-country-level-national-line-headcount-.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = int(params['start_year'])
    y1 = int(params['end_year'])
    s = data[code]
    names = data['names']
    regions = data['regions']
    rows = []
    for unit in s:
        for c in s[unit]:
            pass
    units = list(s.keys())
    unit = units[0] if units else ''
    ser = s[unit] if unit else {}
    changes = []
    for c in ser:
        if c not in regions:
            continue
        yrs = ser[c] if isinstance(ser[c], dict) else {}
        ys = sorted([int(y) for y in yrs if y0 <= int(y) <= y1])
        if len(ys) < 2:
            continue
        a = yrs[ys[0]] if ys[0] in yrs else yrs[str(ys[0])]
        b = yrs[ys[-1]] if ys[-1] in yrs else yrs[str(ys[-1])]
        changes.append((b - a, c, ys[0], ys[-1], a, b))
    changes.sort()
    n = len(changes)
    facts = {'series': code, 'unit': unit, 'countries_with_two_or_more_obs': n}
    if n == 0:
        return {'facts': facts, 'summary': 'No country has two observations of ' + code + ' between ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + '; the change cannot be read.'}
    vals = [x[0] for x in changes]
    facts['median_change'] = round(statistics.median(vals), 2)
    facts['countries_falling'] = len([v for v in vals if v < 0])
    facts['countries_rising'] = len([v for v in vals if v > 0])
    best = changes[0]
    worst = changes[-1]
    facts['largest_fall_country'] = data['names'].get(best[1], best[1])
    facts['largest_fall'] = round(best[0], 2)
    facts['largest_rise_country'] = data['names'].get(worst[1], worst[1])
    facts['largest_rise'] = round(worst[0], 2)
    summary = ('Between first and last observations within ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ', ' + str(n) + ' countries report ' + code + ' (' + unit + '). The median change is ' + str(facts['median_change']) + '; ' + str(facts['countries_falling']) + ' fall and ' + str(facts['countries_rising']) + ' rise. w-c02-3-4~cedar/writer-2~74.text:
The question for this section is what share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They supply no global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate exists for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and irregular

The indicator is coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population. It rests on household surveys, so survey timing sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2002, 3. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013. The results do not say why, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. Among the years 2000 to 2023 the peak came in 2018, with 47 countries.

After 2018 the count was uneven rather than steadily falling: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reported for 2023. Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion is lower in the smaller 2021 sample

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was computed for 2015, 2018 and 2021. These are the first year of the goals, the year of peak reporting and a later year with 30 countries; 2022, with 17 countries, was too thin to use. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285, the Theil index 0.2032 and the coefficient of variation 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. The 2021 sample is smaller and the countries differ between years, so a narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The between-region share of inequality differs by year

Decomposing the Theil index by region, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of it in 2015, 28.8 per cent in 2018 and 21.4 per cent in 2021. In 2015 most of the measured inequality lay between regions; in 2018 and 2021 most lay among countries within the same region. Because the sample changed between years, the size of any real shift is uncertain. The pattern is better read as a warning about which countries are missing than as evidence of regional convergence.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which reported figures can be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while this indicator counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding concerns the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse and irregular, and only 17 countries reported in 2022 against 47 in 2018. The related indicator, social insurance coverage in the poorest quintile, had 1 reporting country in 2023, which supports no statement about the world.

proposals: Governments and statistical offices should run the social protection module of household surveys on a fixed cycle, so that the same countries are observed repeatedly and coverage can be tracked as a panel.
The custodian agencies should publish a numerical threshold for 'substantial coverage' under target 1.3, so that reported figures can be judged against it.

Analysts should report the regional decomposition of coverage inequality only for a fixed set of countries, since the between-region share moved with sample composition from 74.1 per cent in 2015 to 21.4 per cent in 2021.

w-c02-5-4~cedar/writer-1~80.text:
### The series counts displacement, not people affected or losses

This section cannot state how many people were affected by disasters, nor what losses followed. The World Development Indicators supply one series that bears on the question: new displacement associated with disasters, counted in cases. It records no monetary losses, deaths or damage to livelihoods. It counts displacement events, not distinct people, so a person displaced twice in a year may appear twice. It carries no information on income, so it cannot show how many of those displaced were poor. Of Target 1.5, which asks for the exposure and vulnerability of the poor to climate-related extreme events and other shocks to be reduced, the series speaks only to exposure, and only in the form of displacement cases. Resilience and vulnerability are not measured here.

Globally, new disaster displacement stood at 19,188,817 cases in 2015 and 26,393,278 cases in 2023. The two end points should not be read as a smooth trend, because displacement depends heavily on the severity of events in a given year. Reporting coverage also changed, as discussed below, so the rise is not a firm finding of worsening exposure.

### Regional movements diverge

East Asia and Pacific recorded 8,304,660 cases in 2015 and 9,038,561 cases in 2023, the highest regional figure in both years. South Asia moved the other way, from 6,877,900 cases in 2015 to 2,446,054 cases in 2023. A fall of this size may reflect the particular events of the two years rather than a durable gain in resilience, and the series alone cannot separate the two.

Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 1,108,287 cases in 2015 to 6,029,739 cases in 2023, the largest absolute rise of any region. Europe and Central Asia rose from 56,782 cases in 2016 to 4,275,239 cases in 2023, a far larger proportional rise, but the start year is 2016 because no 2015 figure is given, so the comparison is over a different period. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan grouping rose from 1,212,730 cases in 2015 to 2,481,660 cases in 2023. Latin America and the Caribbean changed little, from 1,543,360 cases to 1,728,025 cases. North America rose from 76,000 cases to 394,000 cases, a large proportional increase from a small base.

These counts show where recorded displacement was higher in 2023 than in the earlier year; they do not show who was displaced, and wider reporting may explain part of any rise. The data do not allow a statement that the poor were the people affected.

### Reporting coverage limits comparison

The number of countries reporting changed considerably. It was 112 in 2015, 133 in 2017, 141 in 2018 and 142 in 2020, dipped to 133 in 2021, and was 144 in 2022 and 145 in 2023. Across all years, 199 countries have reported at least once. Some of the global rise from 2015 to 2023 may therefore come from wider reporting, so the global figures are not a like-for-like comparison.

### Spread among countries widened in the reported sample

Among reporting countries, weighted by population, the Gini coefficient was 0.5701 in 2015 and 0.6783 in 2023. The Theil index rose from 0.7232 to 0.8935 and the coefficient of variation from 1.1066 to 1.4691. All three measures point the same way: within the reporting sample, displacement is spread more unevenly in 2023 than in 2015. The sample grew from 112 countries to 145, so part of this change may arise from who reports and not from events.

The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 0.7075 in 2015 to 0.5301 in 2023. This suggests that differences among countries within regions matter more than before, though the change in sample makes the reading tentative.

### Proposals

See the proposals listed below.

claims.fact: c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-5.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2023
c02-5.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Countries should report disaster displacement as distinct people, disaggregated by income or poverty status, so that exposure of the poor under Target 1.5 can be measured.
Statistical agencies should add series on disaster deaths and economic and livelihood losses to the indicators used for Goal 1, since displacement alone cannot answer the question of losses.
Analysts should compare displacement only across a fixed panel of countries that report in every year, so that changes in coverage are not read as changes in exposure.
Planners should examine country-level displacement within regions as well as regional totals, treating this as a hypothesis to test once the reporting sample is stable.

Displacement is counted in cases, not distinct people. Coverage changed from 112 countries in 2015 to 145 in 2023, Europe and Central Asia lacks a 2015 value, and the series says nothing on resilience or vulnerability.

t-country-level-coverage-values-for-the-.code:
def tool(data, params):
    code = params['series']
    y0 = params['start_year']
    y1 = params['end_year']
    s = data[code]
    regions = data['regions']
    names = data['names']
    panel = []
    observed0 = 0
    observed1 = 0
    for u in s:
        if u not in regions:
            continue
        yrs = s[u]
        a = y0 in yrs and yrs[y0] is not None
        b = y1 in yrs and yrs[y1] is not None
        if a:
            observed0 += 1
        if b:
            observed1 += 1
        if a and b:
            panel.append(u)
    n = len(panel)
    facts = {'series': code, 'start_year': y0, 'end_year': y1, 'countries_observed_start': observed0, 'countries_observed_end': observed1, 'panel_size': n}
    if n == 0:
        return {'facts': facts, 'summary': 'No country has values in both ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ' for ' + code + '; no fixed panel can be formed.'}
    v0 = [s[u][y0] for u in panel]
    v1 = [s[u][y1] for u in panel]
    m0 = statistics.mean(v0)
    m1 = statistics.mean(v1)
    all0 = [s[u][y0] for u in s if u in regions and y0 in s[u] and s[u][y0] is not None]
    all1 = [s[u][y1] for u in s if u in regions and y1 in s[u] and s[u][y1] is not None]
    facts['panel_mean_start'] = round(m0, 3)
    facts['panel_mean_end'] = round(m1, 3)
    facts['panel_mean_change'] = round(m1 - m0, 3)
    facts['all_observed_mean_start'] = round(statistics.mean(all0), 3)
    facts['all_observed_mean_end'] = round(statistics.mean(all1), 3)
    facts['all_observed_mean_change'] = round(statistics.mean(all1) - statistics.mean(all0), 3)
    facts['panel_median_change'] = round(statistics.median([b - a for a, b in zip(v0, v1)]), 3)
    facts['countries_rising'] = len([1 for a, b in zip(v0, v1) if b > a])
    facts['countries_falling'] = len([1 for a, b in zip(v0, v1) if b < a])
    summary = 'For ' + code + ', ' + str(n) + ' countries are observed in both ' + str(y0) + ' and ' + str(y1) + ' (' + str(observed0) + ' observed in the first year, ' + str(observed1) + ' in the last). The fixed-panel mean moves from ' + str(round(m0, 3)) + ' to ' + str(round(m1, 3)) + ', a change of ' + str(round(m1 - m0, 3)) + ' in the series unit; the mean over all observed countries changes by ' + str(round(statistics.mean(all1) - statistics.mean(all0), 3)) + '. The gap between the two figures reflects changes in who is observed. Countries without both years are excluded, and unweighted means ignore population size.'
    return {'facts': facts, 'summary': summary}

call.task: To write a global analysis of the Sustainable Development Goals with proposals, as a book of about 560 two-column pages (some 470 of prose and the rest a statistical annex and an account of how the book was made), from the World Bank's World Development Indicators, with base year 2015 and target year 2030; every number traceable to its data, every analysis replicated, every section reviewed.

reasons.charter-1-cooperative: A standing secretariat serves all members equally and keeps the shared bench and shelf continuous across rounds. Admitting tools by two thirds protects the bench from capture without letting one member block useful analysis. Review by two guild peers of other origins matches the cooperative's practice of drafting from replicated analyses. Adopting the book by unanimity mirrors the consent rule of this conference, so that no community is bound to a book it has not accepted.
reasons.charter-1-forum: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps any one community from settling into control of an organisation that has no authority above it. Admitting tools by two thirds protects the shared bench from capture without handing a veto to any single member. First review by those the goals concern tests whether each section serves the people it describes, which is the purpose of a global analysis with proposals. Adopting the book by two thirds lets roughly 560 pages be finished in reasonable time whil
reasons.charter-1-guild: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps any one community from holding the pen, which suits a conference with no authority above its members. Admitting a tool to the shared bench by two thirds protects the bench from a single veto while still requiring broad trust. First review by two guild reviewers of other origins matches the guild's method: an analysis is used only after an analyst of another origin has replicated it. Adoption of the book by unanimity matches the conference's own consent
reasons.charter-1-commons: A chair rotating every twelve rounds keeps every member equal and leaves no standing body above the communities, which suits an order of commons. Admitting tools to the shared bench by two thirds protects the shelf and the bench from capture by a bare majority without letting a single member block necessary work. am-commons-1.title: The shelf of series: how each section's data were chosen and checked
am-commons-1.question: Which World Development Indicators series underlie each section, who gathered them, who checked them, and where did the two disagree?
am-commons-1.why: The commons' mission is a shelf of series chosen by one gatherer and checked by another of a different origin; the book should document that provenance so that every finding's number, year and unit can be traced.

am-commons-2.question: What share of the $100 billion climate finance commitment can the World Development Indicators measure, and what do the available series show?
am-commons-2.why: The World Development Indicators do not carry a direct climate finance series; the heading asserts a finding the bench's tools may not support, and the gap must be stated rather than presumed.

am-commons-3.why: Food loss has no adequate series in the World Development Indicators; the gap belongs in c28 section 2 rather than in a section without data.

am-commons-4.why: Regional chapters omit any treatment of small island developing states, whose data gaps are the widest; if no chapter is added, the 'data gaps and outlook' sections should name them explicitly. The proposal is offered as a reading of coverage, not a new region.

am-guild-1.title: Every finding is replicated on the shared bench by an analyst of another origin
am-guild-1.question: Which of the book's findings were reproduced by an independent analyst from the same World Development Indicators series, and where did the replications diverge?
am-guild-1.why: The guild's mission requires every plan of analyses to be run on the shared bench and replicated before a writer uses it. The book should report the replication record and its discrepancies openly, since this is the basis of its exactness.

am-guild-2.title: Method: indicators, aggregates, years and the reading of targets
am-guild-2.question: How are regional and world aggregates, reference years, units and ambiguous targets handled consistently across the chapters?
am-guild-2.why: A single five-page overview cannot fix the conventions that every finding depends on, such as base year, latest year, weighting and treatment of missing values. Without them, findings across chapters will not be comparable or replicable.

am-guild-3.question: Which cross-goal associations survive replication with alternative country samples, years and controls, and which do not?
am-guild-3.why: Correlations across national data are the findings most likely to be fragile. The section should test their robustness rather than only state limits in general terms.

am-guild-4.why: Mobile phone ownership as an enabling technology is already covered in c10 section 8 and c18 section 5. The pages are better spent on method and replication.

am-cooperative-1.title: How each finding was replicated, reviewed and adopted
am-cooperative-1.question: By what procedure were the book's analyses replicated by the guild and its sections revised until adopted, and what does that procedure guarantee about each stated number, year and unit?
am-cooperative-1.why: The cooperative drafts only from replicated analyses; readers need a short, exact account of replication and adoption so that every finding's provenance is checkable.

am-cooperative-2.title: Findings that did not replicate or that depend on the reading of a target
am-cooperative-2.question: Which candidate findings failed replication or changed under alternative readings of a target, and how large were the differences?
am-cooperative-2.why: Reporting non-replicated or reading-dependent results states the book's limits plainly, as house style requires where data are missing or targets are ambiguous.

am-cooperative-3.question: Mobile phone and internet use differ between women and men, and the World Development Indicators measure that gap in few countries.
am-cooperative-3.why: The draft heading treats mobile phones as enabling by assumption; the section should state a measurable gap and its coverage limits, a claim that can be replicated.

am-cooperative-4.why: Tourism's economic weight is a minor target, poorly covered in the indicators and largely duplicated by the growth and resource sections; the pages are better spent on replicable core findings.

am-forum-1.title: Leaving No One Behind: Who the Averages Hide
am-forum-1.question: Which groups (the poorest quintile, rural dwellers, women and girls, persons with disabilities, displaced people, the old and the very young) fall furthest from the targets, and where do the World Development Indicators fail to disaggregate them?
am-forum-1.why: The pledge to leave no one behind is the agenda's central promise, yet the outline reports national and regional averages almost throughout. A chapter on disaggregated results, stating where the data do not permit disaggregation, is the forum's core concern and fills a gap no other chapter covers.

am-forum-2.question: Women's ownership of mobile phones and accounts, and the gender gap in access, where measured.
am-forum-2.why: The draft heading frames technology for its own sake. Target 5.b concerns women's empowerment, so the section should measure the gap between women and men, and state plainly how few countries report it.

am-forum-3.why: Tourism's economic weight concerns sector output rather than the people the goals address. Its two pages serve readers better in the new chapter on those left behind.

am-forum-4.title: Proposals judged against those they concern
am-forum-4.question: How each community's proposals would affect the poorest and most excluded groups, and what is uncertain in that judgement.
am-forum-4.why: Proposals are written by expert communities. A short cross-check against the groups affected tests whether what is proposed serves them, which is the forum's mission and a safeguard of the book's quality.

w-c02-1-1.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030. The target text quoted in the framework refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices, expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a higher, revised line than the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which the trend tool uses as its goal.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. Projected along its own 2015 to 2024 path, the world ratio would reach 8.365 per cent in 2030. The trend tool rates this as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and gives a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.376. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration. North America starts from a low level, so the slow pace there reflects a small remaining headcount more than a large one.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of four years, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions with nine years of data.

Two regions fall short in a different way. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved the wrong way, from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent, a ratio of -0.481 and a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent. Sub-Saharan Africa and this group are therefore where the world's gap to zero is widest and growing least tractable.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent. Nearly a quarter of assessed countries are therefore moving away from the target, and the share of population in regression is larger than that in stagnation and marginal progress combined only in part: 17.88 per cent against 13.45 per cent.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each period is slower than the one before. At the latest pace, the remaining 10.1 per cent would not reach zero by 2030.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean. Poverty is becoming more concentrated in fewer places rather than evenly shrinking.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. Reporting then ranged between 70 and 93 countries a year to 2022, with 93 in 2018, and fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values are thus largely estimated or modelled from a small number of recent surveys, and no regional values are given for 2025. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 are made with that caution.

### Proposals

The proposals that follow from these findings are addressed to the actors named in each.

Treat the slowing pace since 2021 as a signal for review and plan on the basis that current policy leaves a global headcount well above zero in 2030.
w-c02-1-1.gaps: The series is the $3.00 a day line in 2021 purchasing power parity, not the $1.25 line in the target text. Only 26 countries reported in 2024 and 4 in 2025, so recent values are thinly supported. South Asia has data only from 2020. w-c02-2-1.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and 15 did in 2001. The number rose to 22 in 2002 and 21 in 2003, then to 36 in 2004 and 41 in 2005.

Across the years 2006 to 2008 the count held at 40 each year. It reached 47 in 2009 and 50 in 2010, then stood at 49 in 2011 and 50 in 2012. It fell to 45 in 2013 and 46 in 2014. In 2015, the baseline year of the goals, 55 countries reported, followed by 57 in 2016 and 53 in 2017. The peak came later: 67 in 2018, 62 in 2019, 57 in 2020 and 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much. The indicator has no aggregate series, so no global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008 and 33 in 2009, then jumped to 69 in 2010. It stood at 61 in 2011, 71 in 2012, 61 in 2013 and 69 in 2014.

The count reached 74 in 2015, 72 in 2016 and 67 in 2017, with a high of 84 in 2018. It then fell to 71 in 2019, 58 in 2020, 69 in 2021 and 63 in 2022. The last years are sparse: 48 countries in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. The multidimensional series is somewhat better populated than the national-line series in the middle years, but both lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. The classification should be read with that ambiguity in mind: a national line is set by each country, and it may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

The split is therefore not even. Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, which shows that large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. The population shares describe only the countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.649 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line as well.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other. The national and international lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of 0.025885 with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The coefficient is positive. Given the setup of the test, this does not indicate that countries with higher starting headcounts fell faster. The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence rather than catching up.

### Proposals

The findings lead to the proposals listed below.

proposals: Statistical offices and their funders should prioritise the timely publication of national-line headcounts, so that the 2023 to 2025 reporting counts of 40, 31 and 13 countries are filled in before the 2030 assessment.
Countries should publish the national poverty line in force for each survey year and flag any revision, so that changes in definition can be separated from changes in poverty.
Monitoring bodies should report national-line and international-line results side by side, since the two move together in level but only loosely in change.
Attention and support should be directed to the 34 countries in regression, and to the widening spread among the 25 countries in the convergence sample.
w-c02-2-1.gaps: The data give no aggregate for either the national-line or the multidimensional headcount, so no global or regional rate can be stated. Coverage of recent years is thin, and the trend classes rest on 94 countries only. National lines differ in definition and may be revised, and no numeric halving target is set in the assessment. The comparison with the $3.00 line covers 21 countries and the convergence test 25. Poverty in all its dimensions by national definitions, including by sex and age, is not covered here.

w-c02-4-1.text:
Access to basic services is the plainest test of target 1.4, which asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated, and they are drawn from the World Bank's World Development Indicators. They measure coverage of the population, not the income of those covered, so they show where service gaps lie and not directly who among the poor is excluded.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. The regional spread is wide. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is projected to reach 59.4914% in 2030, which leaves roughly four in ten rural residents without basic water even if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water everywhere

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met, holding 46.64% of the assessed population share. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access is closing the gap but not in Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%, the fastest regional gain in annual rate yet still the lowest level. Its projected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed, and Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, resting on the regional pattern above and on the limits of national averages.

Access to land, property, inheritance and financial services, also named in target 1.4, is not covered here.

w-c02-6-1.text:
### Education spending has slipped as a share of budgets

Government expenditure on education, measured as a share of total government expenditure, shows little movement at the global level and a drift downward in most regions. The world figure was 14.1095% in 2015 and 13.9646% in 2023. The small global change conceals larger regional shifts. East Asia & Pacific fell from 15.1455% in 2015 to 12.9541% in 2023. South Asia fell from 13.8682% in 2015 to 11.3173% in 2025. North America fell from 12.9491% in 2015 to 10.6536% in 2022, and Europe & Central Asia from 11.8212% in 2015 to 11.685% in 2022.

The regions with the highest shares have also lost ground, with one exception. Sub-Saharan Africa spent 16.9629% in 2015 and 15.3772% in 2024. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan fell from 15.1596% in 2016 to 13.1015% in 2022. Latin America & Caribbean rose slightly, from 16.4395% in 2015 to 16.557% in 2024. A share of the budget is not an amount per child, and it says nothing about whether spending reaches the poorest households. The end years also differ by region, so the comparisons are not over identical periods. For 2025, only 60 countries report, so the latest South Asian figure rests on thin coverage.

### Health spending is lowest where need is greatest

Domestic general government health expenditure, as a share of general government expenditure, differs widely between regions. North America stood at 22.1201% in 2015 and 22.7676% in 2023. Europe & Central Asia was at 14.9714% in 2015 and 14.5127% in 2023. Latin America & Caribbean moved from 11.4856% in 2015 to 11.8404% in 2023.

South Asia remains far below the others, though it improved from 3.652% in 2015 to 4.8035% in 2022. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 10.8947% in 2015 to 11.3024% in 2019, and the series ends there in the regional view, so later change cannot be judged. The gap between North America and South Asia in the latest years shown is large, and the rise in South Asia leaves it well short of every other region listed.

Coverage of this indicator is good until recently. Countries reporting numbered 191 in 2015, 193 in 2019 and 192 in 2023, and 193 countries reported in at least one year. Only 7 countries reported for 2024, so 2023 is the last year with broad coverage. Regional aggregates exist for five regions only: Europe & Central Asia, Latin America & Caribbean, North America, South Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa. East Asia & Pacific and the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan are absent from the regional figures.

### Aid has grown, and most of it goes to a few regions

Net official development assistance and official aid received rose from US$146,601,921,875 in 2015 to US$202,111,656,250 in 2021 for the world. Sub-Saharan Africa received the largest regional amount: US$44,772,349,948 in 2015 and US$62,285,599,988 in 2021. Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan saw the steepest increase, from US$19,311,190,262 to US$34,886,630,493 over the same years.

Other regions received less and grew more slowly. East Asia & Pacific went from US$8,525,499,852 to US$10,515,909,809. Europe & Central Asia went from US$8,548,860,034 to US$9,729,970,041. Latin America & Caribbean went from US$10,133,120,065 to US$11,848,990,025. South Asia went from US$15,700,559,961 to US$17,641,809,914. North America's series is trivial, at US$59,999.9987 in 2000 and US$90,000.0036 in 2004, and is not a meaningful comparator. These figures are in current dollars, so part of the growth reflects prices, and the series does not distinguish aid aimed at poverty reduction from aid for other purposes. In 2023, 136 countries reported, but the regional series stop at 2021.

### Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified

Target 1.b calls for pro-poor and gender-sensitive policy frameworks. One available measure is the share of social protection and labour benefits that reach the poorest fifth of the population. Reporting is sparse and erratic. Only 1 country reported in 2000, 11 in 2005 and 28 in 2008. The count peaked at 46 in 2018, then fell to 35 in 2019, 23 in 2020, 30 in 2021, 17 in 2022 and 1 in 2023. In all, 123 countries reported in at least one year, and no aggregates exist. A global or regional trend therefore cannot be computed from these data.

The targets can be read in more than one way. Target 1.a asks for resources that are adequate and predictable, but the indicators here measure totals and shares, not adequacy or predictability. Spending shares and aid totals can show direction and scale. They cannot show whether the money reached people in poverty.

### Proposals

The evidence supports several proposals, set out below.

claims.fact: c02-6.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2016
c02-6.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2022
c02-6.r5: countries reporting in any year
c02-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-6.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2021
c02-6.r4: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Countries and statistical agencies should report the share of budgets spent on education and health alongside spending per person, so that falling shares can be told apart from falling real resources.
Donors should publish aid by purpose, separating poverty-reduction spending from other aid, so that growth in totals can be tied to Target 1.a.
South Asia's health spending share, still far below other regions, should be a priority for domestic budget reform and targeted support.
Statistical agencies should fund regular household surveys so that benefit incidence for the poorest fifth is reported by many more countries each year.
w-c02-6-1.gaps: The data do not show spending per person, real-terms changes, or whether spending reached poor households. Aid is not split by purpose or by least developed country status, and the regional aid series end in 2021. Health aggregates are missing for two regions, and latest-year coverage is thin for education in 2025 and health in 2024. Benefit incidence for the poorest fifth has no aggregates and erratic country coverage. Gender-sensitive policy under Target 1.b is not measured by any series used here.

w-c02-3-1.text:
The question for this section is what share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot yet answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They do not supply a global coverage level for the poorest quintile. No regional or world aggregate is available for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and uneven

Coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, measured as a percentage of that quintile, rests on household surveys. Survey timing therefore sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000 two countries reported, and in 2002 three. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013, a drop that reflects survey cycles rather than any change in policy. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. The peak came in 2018, with 47 countries. Thereafter the count declined: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only one country reported for 2023.

Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The figure shows that the indicator has some historical reach, but in any single year fewer than half of those countries are observed. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion narrows as the sample shrinks

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was measured for three years. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285 and the Theil index 0.2032. The coefficient of variation was 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini fell to 0.2056, the Theil index to 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation to 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. That reading needs care. The 2021 sample is smaller than the 2015 and 2018 samples, and the countries differ between years. A narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence in coverage. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries, and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The regional share of inequality changes sharply

The decomposition of the Theil index by region shows a larger shift. In 2015, regional differences accounted for 74.1 per cent of the Theil index, expressed in the data as 0.7408. By 2018 the between-region share was 0.2878, and by 2021 it was 0.2137. In 2015, then, most of the inequality in coverage lay between regions. By 2018 and 2021 most of it lay among countries within the same region.

The change is large enough to suggest that the composition of the sample, not only the policies of governments, drives the result. Regions represented by few countries in 2015 may have been better represented later, which would shift the weight from the between-region to the within-region component. The data given here do not allow that explanation to be tested.

### Social insurance coverage is almost unobserved

A related indicator, coverage of social insurance programmes in the poorest quintile, was queried for 2023. Only one country reported. A single observation supports no comparison and no statement about the world. Social insurance, which includes contributory pensions and unemployment benefits, is the kind of protection that often misses people in informal work, but the data here cannot show whether that is so.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which the reported figures could be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while the indicator examined here counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding for this section is therefore about the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse, irregular and declining in recent reporting.

claims.fact: c02-3.r1: countries reporting in any year

proposals: Governments and statistical offices should field the household surveys that measure social protection coverage on a regular cycle, so that at least the countries reporting in 2018 report again in each later survey round.

The World Bank and partner agencies should publish regional and world aggregates for coverage in the poorest quintile, with the sample of countries stated, so that progress on target 1.3 can be read at all.
The custodians of the indicator framework should define substantial coverage as a numerical threshold for the poorest quintile, so that reported figures can be judged against it.
w-c02-3-1.gaps: The data give no global or regional level of coverage for the poorest quintile, only the number of reporting countries and the spread among them. The samples differ between years, so trends cannot be separated from changes in who is observed. Social insurance coverage is observed for one country in 2023. The data do not capture the adequacy or quality of benefits, informal or non-survey support, or protection for the vulnerable beyond the poorest fifth. Target 1.3 does not define substantial coverage numerically.

w-c02-1-2.text:
### The world headcount in 2015 and 2024

Target 1.1 asks for the eradication of extreme poverty for all people everywhere by 2030. The target text in the framework refers to a line of $1.25 a day. The series available to the bench is different: the poverty headcount ratio at $3.00 a day in 2021 purchasing power parity prices, expressed as a percentage of population. The figures below therefore describe a higher, revised line than the one named in the target, and the two cannot be read as the same measure. Eradication is also open to more than one reading. Here it is treated as a headcount of 0.0 per cent, which the trend tool uses as its goal.

On that series the world headcount ratio stood at 13.4 per cent of the population in 2015 and at 10.1 per cent in 2024. The fall is real, but it is far from zero. Projected along its own 2015 to 2024 path, the world ratio would reach 8.365 per cent in 2030. The trend tool rates this as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed, and gives a ratio of progress to the required pace of 0.376. The target is not on course to be met at the global level.

### Regional paths diverge

The world average conceals very different regional courses, shown in the figure for result c02-1.r1. East Asia and Pacific fell from 6.1 per cent in 2015 to 2.0 per cent in 2024. Europe and Central Asia fell from 1.2 per cent to 0.6 per cent. North America moved from 1.1 per cent to 0.9 per cent. Latin America and the Caribbean fell from 6.0 per cent to 4.3 per cent.

The trend classification separates these regions. East Asia and Pacific, with a ratio of 0.844 and an expected 2030 value of 0.951 per cent, shows moderate progress but needs acceleration. Europe and Central Asia, at a ratio of 0.685 and an expected 0.378 per cent, falls in the same class. Latin America and the Caribbean, with a ratio of 0.426 and an expected 3.4436 per cent in 2030, and North America, with a ratio of 0.284 and an expected 0.7873 per cent, show only marginal progress and need significant acceleration. North America starts from a low level, so the slow pace there reflects a small remaining headcount.

South Asia is the one region classed as on track or target met. Its series begins in 2020 rather than 2015, at 9.4 per cent, and reaches 2.6 per cent in 2024. The ratio of 0.96 and the expected 2030 value of 0.3782 per cent rest on a window of four years, so the verdict is less secure than those for regions with nine years of data.

Two regions fall short in a different way. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 45.4 per cent in 2015 to 45.0 per cent in 2024, a ratio of 0.015, which the trend tool classes as stagnation; its expected 2030 value is 44.7353 per cent. The Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group moved the wrong way, from 11.3 per cent to 14.3 per cent, a ratio of -0.481 and a classification of regression, with an expected 2030 value of 16.7305 per cent.

### Country patterns and the slowing pace

Among 105 countries assessed, 18 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 45.55 per cent of the population of the assessed countries. Another 41 show moderate progress, with 23.11 per cent of the population, and 15 show marginal progress, with 11.25 per cent. Seven countries are stagnant, with 2.2 per cent, and 24 are in regression, with 17.88 per cent. Of the 105 countries assessed, 24 are therefore moving away from the target.

The pace of the world decline has slowed. The break analysis for the world series finds breaks in 2014 and 2021. The mean annual change was -1.59231 percentage points over 2001 to 2013, -0.88 over 2014 to 2018, and -0.325 over 2021 to 2024. Each period is slower than the one before. No projection of zero from the latest pace is computed here, and the 2030 value of 8.365 per cent above is the only projected figure.

Countries are also not drawing together. Across 49 countries, the convergence test for 2015 to 2022 gives a beta of -0.012703 with a p-value of 0.1794 and an R squared of 0.0469, so no reliable tendency of high-poverty countries to fall faster is found. The coefficient of variation rose from 1.9775 in 2015 to 2.4544 in 2022, which means the spread between countries widened relative to the mean.

### Reporting coverage limits confidence

The latest values rest on thin reporting. Across all years 168 countries have reported at least once, and 87 reported in 2015. From 2015 onwards the count peaked at 93 in 2018, then fell to 73 in 2022, 60 in 2023, 26 in 2024 and 4 in 2025. The 2024 regional values therefore rest on far fewer reporting countries than those for 2015, and no regional values are given for 2025. Comparisons between 2015 and 2024 should be made with that caution.

### Proposals

The proposals are listed below.

claims.fact: c02-1.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2015
c02-1.r1: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan 2024
c02-1.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan ratio
c02-1.r3: Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan expected 2030
c02-1.r4: countries on track or target met
c02-1.r4: population share on track or target met
c02-1.r4: countries moderate progress, but acceleration needed
c02-1.r4: population share moderate progress, but acceleration needed
c02-1.r4: countries marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed
c02-1.r4: population share marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed
c02-1.r2: countries reporting in any year

proposals: National statistical offices and the World Bank should prioritise household surveys in the countries and regions with the oldest or missing data, so that the 2024 and 2025 headcounts rest on more than a few reporting countries.

Development finance partners should concentrate poverty-reduction support on Sub-Saharan Africa and on the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan group, where the headcount is stagnant or rising.
The Sustainable Development Goals monitoring community should state in its reporting which poverty line is used and that the $3.00 a day line is not the $1.25 a day line named in target 1.1.
Governments in the 24 countries classed as in regression should publish national plans that set out why poverty is rising and what measures would reverse it.
w-c02-1-2.gaps: The series is the $3.00 a day line in 2021 prices, not the $1.25 line in the target text. Eradication is read as 0.0 per cent. Regional values for 2024 rest on 26 reporting countries and none exist for 2025. South Asia has data only from 2020. Projections extend each region's own past path and are not forecasts. The data give no causes for the regional divergence, no count of people, and no measure of depth or severity of poverty.

w-c02-2-2.text:
### Coverage of national poverty lines is thin and uneven

Target 1.2 asks for a halving, by 2030, of the proportion of people living in poverty according to national definitions. The indicator that measures it, the poverty headcount ratio at national poverty lines (% of population), is reported by 161 countries in at least one year. That figure overstates what is available at any moment. In 2000 only 16 countries reported a value, and in 2005 the count was 41. It reached 55 in 2015, the baseline year of the goals, and peaked at 72 in 2021.

The recent years thin out sharply. Only 52 countries reported in 2022, 40 in 2023, 31 in 2024 and 13 in 2025. The latest observations are therefore the least complete, and any reading of the decade to 2030 rests on a shrinking set of countries. Reporting lags are part of the cause, but the data do not say how much.

The indicator has no aggregate series. No global or regional national-line headcount can be read from it, so the data given here do not support a statement of how the headcount changed worldwide. Change can be described only country by country, as in the next section.

### Multidimensional measures show a similar pattern

Target 1.2 speaks of poverty in all its dimensions, and the multidimensional poverty headcount ratio (World Bank) (% of population) is the nearest companion indicator. It was reported by 158 countries in any year. Coverage began at 26 countries in 2008, reached 74 in 2015 and peaked at 84 in 2018. It then fell to 63 in 2022, 48 in 2023, 23 in 2024 and 4 in 2025.

Like the national-line series, it has no aggregate. It is better populated in most middle years, but both series lose coverage towards the present.

### Progress toward the target is divided

The trend assessment covers 94 countries and sets no numeric target, since a halving depends on each country's own baseline and definition. A national line is set by each country and may be revised, so a change in the headcount can reflect a change in the definition as well as in living conditions. Shares below are given to one decimal place.

Of the 94 countries assessed, 41 are on track or have met the target, and they hold 63.8% of the population of the assessed group. A further 7 countries show moderate progress but need acceleration, covering 3.8% of that population. Another 7 show marginal progress and need significant acceleration, covering 4.4%. Five countries are stagnating, with 2.1% of the population. Regression is recorded in 34 countries, with 26.0% of the population.

Fewer than half the countries, 41 of 94, are on track, yet they account for nearly two thirds of the assessed population, so large countries weigh heavily in the result. At the same time, 34 countries are moving the wrong way, and they contain more than a quarter of the assessed population. These shares describe only countries with enough data to be classified; they are not shares of the world.

### National and international lines move together only in part

A comparison with the headcount at $3.00 a day (2021 PPP) covers 21 countries from 2015 to 2022. The rank correlation of 2022 levels is 0.6486 by Spearman and 0.5096 by Kendall. Countries with high poverty by their own line therefore tend to have high poverty by the international line.

The link is weaker for change. The Spearman correlation of changes is 0.3763 and the Kendall value is 0.2638. A country's movement on one measure is only loosely related to its movement on the other, so the two lines are not interchangeable for tracking progress, and the sample of 21 countries is small.

### Dispersion has widened

A convergence test across 25 countries for 2015 to 2022 regresses each country's change in headcount on its starting level. A negative coefficient would mean that countries starting higher fell faster. The estimated beta is 0.025885, with a p-value of 0.0008 and an R squared of 0.2588. The positive sign means that higher starting headcounts were associated with larger increases or smaller falls, not catching up.

The coefficient of variation rose from 0.4773 in 2015 to 0.5778 in 2022, so the spread of national headcounts widened relative to their mean in this group. The evidence from these 25 countries points to divergence, though the group is small and may not represent all countries.

### Proposals

The proposals below follow from the coverage gaps and the divergence found above.

c02-2.r5: countries reporting in any year
c02-2.r2: countries on track or target met
c02-2.r2: population share on track or target met
c02-2.r2: countries moderate progress, but acceleration needed
c02-2.r2: population share moderate progress, but acceleration needed
c02-2.r2: countries marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed
c02-2.r2: population share marginal progress, and significant acceleration needed

proposals: National statistical offices should publish national-line headcounts within two years of survey fieldwork, so that the latest years are no longer the thinnest.
Countries that revise a national poverty line should publish a back-cast series on the old and new definitions, so that a change in the headcount can be told apart from a change in the line.
Monitoring bodies should report national-line and international-line headcounts side by side, since their changes are only loosely related.
Convergence should be tracked on a fixed group of countries each year, as the widening spread of headcounts is a signal that needs follow-up in the next survey rounds.
w-c02-2-2.gaps: The indicators have no aggregate series, so no global or regional change in national-line poverty can be stated. Coverage falls steeply after 2021, and the trend classes cover 94 countries, the link test 21 and the convergence test 25. Population shares refer only to assessed countries. No numeric target is set, and national lines differ and may be revised, so headcounts are not strictly comparable across countries or over time. The data give no cause for reporting lags or for divergence.

w-c02-4-2.text:
Target 1.4 asks that the poor and the vulnerable have equal access to basic services. The indicators used here come from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and cover rural populations, where deprivation is concentrated. They measure coverage of a whole rural population, not the income of those covered. They therefore show where service gaps lie, but they cannot show directly whether the poor within a region are reached. That limit applies to every finding below.

### Drinking water gains are real but uneven

Rural use of at least basic drinking water services across the world rose from 78.7253% of the rural population in 2015 to 84.5029% in 2024, with 168 countries reporting in 2024. Sub-Saharan Africa moved from 44.3456% to 52.8948%, while North America reached 99.8527% and Europe & Central Asia 95.5668%. South Asia rose from 88.2444% to 95.2211%, and East Asia & Pacific from 83.3706% to 91.1148%.

Against a target of 100% by 2030, the world trend is classed as marginal progress, with significant acceleration needed; the expected world value for 2030 is 88.5883%. North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target. Sub-Saharan Africa is also classed as marginal, with an expected 2030 value of 59.4914%, which leaves about 40.5% of its rural population without basic water if the present pace holds.

### Sanitation lags water in most regions

Rural basic sanitation rose globally from 57.5406% in 2015 to 71.9486% in 2024, with 159 countries reporting. South Asia made the largest gain, from 50.4934% to 79.8838%, and East Asia & Pacific rose from 73.909% to 90.9641%. Sub-Saharan Africa advanced only from 21.8442% to 27.0945%, the lowest level of any region. North America slipped from 99.3437% to 98.4369%, a small fall from a very high level. No projected 2030 sanitation value for the regions is available among the results, so the pace of Sub-Saharan Africa is judged here from levels alone.

For the whole population, the sanitation trend classes 49 of 213 countries assessed as on track or target met. The share of the assessed population in these is 46.64%. A further 34 countries show moderate progress, 54 marginal progress, 37 stagnation and 39 regression. Regression covers 13.36% of the population share, so the average improvement conceals a group of countries that are losing ground.

Rural sanitation shows weak convergence across 158 countries: the beta coefficient is -0.007117 (p-value 0.0001), with an R squared of 0.0763. The coefficient of variation fell from 0.4798 in 2015 to 0.4224 in 2024. Countries starting lower tended to gain somewhat faster, yet the low R squared means that initial level explains little of the variation, and the narrowing is slight.

### Electricity access closes the gap except in Sub-Saharan Africa

Rural electricity access rose globally from 76.5936% in 2015 to 84.8934% in 2024, with 210 countries reporting. South Asia went from 81.4025% to 99.8174%, and Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan from 87.5528% to 93.9792%. Sub-Saharan Africa rose from 18.4911% to 35.6988%. Its annual rate of 0.07583 is the highest of any region, yet it is still classed as marginal progress, and the expected 2030 value is 55.3497%. The world trend is moderate progress with acceleration needed. Latin America & Caribbean is classed as marginal, rising only from 89.1221% to 91.026%.

Inequality among countries in rural electricity access fell. The population-weighted Gini coefficient went from 0.169 in 2015 to 0.114 in 2024, and the Theil index from 0.0977 to 0.0628. The between-region share of the Theil index fell from 76.04% to 68.25%, so regional differences still account for most of the remaining inequality.

### Proposals follow from the gaps

The findings point to priorities for the final years of the decade, each resting on the regional pattern above.
