w-c02-3-4.text:
The question for this section is what share of the poorest quintile is covered by social protection and labour programmes. Target 1.3 asks for substantial coverage of the poor and the vulnerable by 2030. The data available through the bench cannot answer the question in the form posed. They show how many countries report coverage for the poorest fifth of the population, and how unevenly the reported coverage is spread among them. They supply no global coverage level for the poorest quintile, and no regional or world aggregate exists for this indicator.

### Reporting is thin and irregular

The indicator is coverage of social safety net programmes in the poorest quintile, expressed as a percentage of that quintile's population. It rests on household surveys, so survey timing sets how many countries appear in any year. In 2000, 2 countries reported, and in 2002, 3. Reporting grew to 11 countries in 2005 and 27 in 2008. It reached 41 countries in 2012, then fell to 24 in 2013. The results do not say why, and the cause is not established here. In 2015, the first year of the goals, 38 countries reported. Among the years 2000 to 2023 the peak came in 2018, with 47 countries.

After 2018 the count was uneven rather than steadily falling: 36 countries in 2019, 24 in 2020, 30 in 2021 and 17 in 2022. Only 1 country reported for 2023. Across all years, 121 countries have reported at least once. The yearly counts are not a panel of the same countries, so a comparison between two years mixes real change with a change in who is observed. No claim about a global trend in coverage can be drawn from these counts alone.

### Dispersion is lower in the smaller 2021 sample

The spread of coverage among reporting countries, weighted by population, was computed for 2015, 2018 and 2021. These are the first year of the goals, the year of peak reporting and a later year with 30 countries; 2022, with 17 countries, was too thin to use. In 2015, with 38 countries, the Gini coefficient was 0.3285, the Theil index 0.2032 and the coefficient of variation 0.5784. In 2018, with 47 countries, the Gini was 0.3157, the Theil index 0.1668 and the coefficient of variation 0.5577. In 2021, with 30 countries, the Gini was 0.2056, the Theil index 0.0942 and the coefficient of variation 0.3912.

On its face, coverage became more evenly distributed among the countries observed. The 2021 sample is smaller and the countries differ between years, so a narrower spread may reflect which countries were surveyed as much as convergence. The measure describes inequality in coverage among countries and says nothing about whether the level of coverage rose.

### The between-region share of inequality differs by year

Decomposing the Theil index by region, differences between regions accounted for 74.1 per cent of it in 2015, 28.8 per cent in 2018 and 21.4 per cent in 2021. In 2015 most of the measured inequality lay between regions; in 2018 and 2021 most lay among countries within the same region. Because the sample changed between years, the size of any real shift is uncertain. The pattern is better read as a warning about which countries are missing than as evidence of regional convergence.

### What follows for target 1.3

Target 1.3 can be read in more than one way. Substantial coverage is not defined as a number, so no threshold exists against which reported figures can be judged. The target also covers floors for all, while this indicator counts only the poorest fifth and only programmes that survey questions capture. The finding concerns the evidence itself: the instrument for tracking the target is sparse and irregular, and only 17 countries reported in 2022 against 47 in 2018. The related indicator, social insurance coverage in the poorest quintile, had 1 reporting country in 2023, which supports no statement about the world.

proposals: Governments and statistical offices should run the social protection module of household surveys on a fixed cycle, so that the same countries are observed repeatedly and coverage can be tracked as a panel.
The custodian agencies should publish a numerical threshold for 'substantial coverage' under target 1.3, so that reported figures can be judged against it.

Analysts should report the regional decomposition of coverage inequality only for a fixed set of countries, since the between-region share moved with sample composition from 74.1 per cent in 2015 to 21.4 per cent in 2021.
w-c02-3-4.gaps: The data give no global or regional level of coverage for the poorest quintile and no aggregate. Reporting countries differ from year to year, so trends cannot be separated from sample change. The reasons for falls in reporting after 2012 and 2018 are not covered. Social insurance coverage has one reporting country in 2023. Vulnerable groups beyond the poorest fifth, programme adequacy and benefit levels are not measured.

(5) The 'Africa' heading overstates: Sub-Saharan Africa is not 'Africa'. (6) The proposal on conflict and population growth has no finding behind it; cut or ground it. The water finding does not answer the question about the poor directly; say so plainly in the findings.

r-w-c02-1-1-quarry/reviewer.comments: Most figures match their facts, but several do not. (3) 'Reporting ranged between 70 and 93 countries a year to 2022' omits 2001 and the 2003 low; the fact set shows 48 in 2001, but the sentence is limited to 2015 onwards, so say so. (4) 'Poverty is becoming more concentrated in fewer places' is not supported by the coefficient of variation; say only that spread widened. (5) The pace claim 'would not reach zero by 2030' has no computed figure. (6) The Proposals heading ends with a stub sentence. Delete it or list the proposals. (7) 'Hardest, growing least tractable' is interpretive. Cut it.

r-w-c02-2-1-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers to correct: Spearman level is 0.6486 in the facts, not 0.649; moderate-progress share is 0.0376, so 3.8% is acceptable but state it as 3.76% or keep consistently rounded; regression share is 25.96%, not 26.0% (26.0% is acceptable only if rounding is stated, and 25.96% rounds to 26.0%, so keep one rounding rule across all shares). Also, the text says 2007 and 2008 counts are covered by 'held at 40', which is correct. Substantive faults: the section never states how headcounts changed (levels or direction by national definition), so the question is only half answered; add that or say the data give no aggregate. r-w-c02-4-1-elm/reviewer.comments: Check numbers against facts. (1) Water: the text calls the world trend 'marginal progress'; this matches r7 (ratio 0.464), but the 59.4914% projection for Sub-Saharan Africa leaves about 40.5% without water, which is fine. (2) 'Sub-Saharan Africa... fastest regional gain in annual rate' for electricity: the r8 rate is 0.07583, but South Asia's is 0.02292, so this holds; however Sub-Saharan Africa's trend is marginal, and this is not stated. r-w-c02-6-1-orchard/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts, but several do not belong to the cited results as used. The health coverage counts (191, 193, 192, 193, 7) come from c02-6.r5 and the 2024 count is filed under r2 in the claims; confirm the right result is cited. r-w-c02-6-1-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts, but several do not read as the results give them. r-w-c02-1-2-quarry/reviewer.comments:
Most numbers match their facts. Problems to correct:

r-w-c02-6-2-orchard/reviewer.comments: S1: the 81 per cent rise is derived, not a fact; it is flagged as own calculation, but 34.89/19.31 gives about 80.7%, so state 'about 81 per cent' only if the derivation is cited. r-w-c02-6-2-elm/reviewer.comments:
Most figures match their facts, but several do not.

S1: '81 per cent' is derived, not a fact (34.89/19.31 is about 80.7 per cent; acceptable only if flagged, as it is). 'US$59,999.9987 in 2000' is a fact but is a trivial series. r-w-c02-3-2-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers check against the facts: counts, Gini, Theil, CV and shares all match (74.1, 28.8, 21.4 per cent round 0.7408, 0.2878, 0.2137). r-w-c02-4-3-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts, but several statements go beyond the results. (1) 'Sub-Saharan Africa rate of 0.07583' is given without a unit or meaning; state it or cut it. (2) 'North America and South Asia are on track or have met the target' omits the Sub-Saharan trend rate caveat; fine, but Europe & Central Asia is also on track for electricity, which is not mentioned. (3) The proposal to 'investigate the 39 countries' is a whole-population sanitation finding, not rural, and the 13.36% is of assessed population; keep the wording but do not tie it to rural gaps. (4) The 'Proposals' section ends with 'listed below' but no list appears in the text; add the three proposals. (5) The opening says urban populations are absent, yet the first proposal ranks water and electricity above sanitation, where Sub-Saharan Africa is weakest (27.0945%); add sanitation. (6) The unsupported claim that deprivation is 'concentrated' in rural areas has no cited fact; cut or qualify it. (7) The section never states that the poor's access is unmeasured in its conclusion.

r-w-c02-6-3-orchard/reviewer.comments: S1: Most figures match their facts. The text gives 'about 81 per cent' for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan rise; it is flagged as derived, which is acceptable, and it is correct (about 80.7). The claim that Sub-Saharan Africa rose by less is also derived and not stated with a figure; give it (about 39 per cent). The 2000 and 2004 North America aid figures are not in the 2015 to 2021 comparison and add little; cut or explain. The 60 countries for 2025 is a fact, but South Asia is a regional figure, so say the count refers to the series and not to South Asia alone. S2: the aid question is answered only by saying the data cannot answer it; the opening sentence on spending as 'essential services' covers education and health only, so name that limit. S3: the proposals are listed but not given in the text; the closing section only points to them. State them there. 'Aid rose in every region' is true for the listed regions but North America is excluded; make the heading say so. S5: the proposals heading is empty; fill it.

r-w-c02-6-3-elm/reviewer.comments: Check against the facts: every figure matches, but some numbers are not facts of cited results. The text says 'about 81 per cent' (derived, flagged as such, which is acceptable), yet the Sub-Saharan Africa rise (about 39 per cent) is only implied; state or drop it. Health reporting years 2000-2018 and the claim 'Countries reporting 2015: 191' are fine. The social protection counts (2015: 37 etc.) are fine. Problems: the education coverage figure of 60 countries is labelled 'countries reporting 2025' but sits under r1; confirm it is for education. The proposal for constant prices and per-child spending rests on stated gaps, but the proposals section lists no proposals in the text, only a pointer; write them out. The heading 'Pro-poor targeting cannot be verified' is declarative, but the education heading 'fell in most regions' ignores Latin America's rise and Europe's flat share; the Sub-Saharan Africa fall is large and should be named. The section answers the question only partly: say plainly that no figure for pro-poor aid exists. Mixed end years (2022 to 2025) weaken comparison; harmonise or flag in one sentence.

r-w-c02-5-2-quarry/reviewer.comments: S1: Facts match, but the text rounds Gini 0.5701 to 0.570, Theil 0.7232 to 0.723 and 0.8935 to 0.893, and Gini 0.6783 to 0.678. Give them as the results do: 0.5701, 0.7232, 0.6783, 0.8935. The 2008-2012 range 'from 60 (2009) to 80 (2008)' is wrong: 2011 is 62 and 2012 is 79 and 2010 is 73, so the range holds, but 2016 (116) and 2019 (136) are omitted without comment; add or drop. S2: The question asks about people affected and losses; the answer is only cases, and the section admits losses are missing. Lead with that and state plainly that no answer on losses is possible. S3: 'Spread widened' is partly sample-driven; soften the proposal on national planning accordingly. 'Most of the unevenness' is fine. The closing 'Proposals' heading holds only one sentence; delete it, since the proposals follow. S5: Heading 'Disaster displacement rose to 26,393,278 cases' overstates given the coverage caveat; qualify it.

r-w-c02-3-3-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers match the facts: counts, Gini, Theil, CV and shares (74.1, 28.8, 21.4 per cent from 0.7408, 0.2878, 0.2137) are correct. Corrections: (1) 'Thereafter the count fell: 36 ... 24 ... 30 ... 17' wrongly implies a steady fall; 2021 (30) rose from 2020 (24). (2) The gaps text cites 'falls in reporting ... after 2018' as unexplained, which is fine, but the 'peak came in 2018' claim is limited to years listed; state the peak is in 2000-2023. (3) 2021 is called 'the latest year with a reasonably large sample', which is a judgement; 2022 had 17 and say so. (4) The 'social insurance' section cites a result for a different indicator without naming its year of query clearly; fold it into gaps. (5) The Theil decomposition is not tied to a proposal; the proposals are generic. (6) Heading 'The regional share of inequality falls' overstates given composition changes; soften. Trim repeated caveats.

r-w-c02-4-4-orchard/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts, but some statements do not follow the results. (1) Sub-Saharan Africa electricity: 'fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale' is unclear and unsupported; South Asia gained 18.4 points against 17.2, so drop or restate. (2) South Asia water is called 'on track or met' while 2024 is 95.2211% and the 2030 value 100.176% is a linear artefact; say so. (3) Sanitation 'by far the lowest' is fine, but the first proposal says 'lowest of any region' while only some regions are shown; name all regions or cite the full set. (4) Electricity: Latin America & Caribbean 'marginal progress' is correct for the 2030 trend, but the world water trend should be stated as 'marginal progress' consistently. (5) The 'Proposals follow from the gaps' section ends with one stub sentence and no proposals; remove or list them. (6) Say that the Gini and Theil are population-weighted across 209-210 countries. (7) The proposal on regressing countries follows from the finding, but the 13.36% is a share of the assessed population, not of rural residents.

r-w-c02-1-4-quarry/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts, with these exceptions. (1) Europe and Central Asia expected 2030 is 0.378, as the fact gives it, but the text also gives South Asia's value as 0.3782; both are correct. (2) The text gives the trend tool's 'Its ratio is 0.376' and the world rate is -0.03092, which is not cited; fine. (3) 'Each reported segment is slower than the one before' holds: -1.59231, -0.88, -0.325. (4) The 2025 reporting count of 4 is correct. Problems: the proposal to 'Direct acceleration effort' to the Middle East group and Sub-Saharan Africa does not follow cleanly from findings, since the data give no causes, and the proposal to fund a study of the 24 regression countries rests on a share (17.88 per cent) not tied to the proposal. The $1.25 line proposal presumes data that the bench does not have; qualify it. The 'Proposals' heading introduces a list the text itself does not show; put the proposals in the body. Where 'mean annual change' appears, add the unit (percentage points). The 2024 world value of 10.1 per cent rests on 26 reporting countries; say so in the finding itself.

r-w-c02-2-4-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers: the population shares are rounded, so 3.8% (fact 0.0376), 4.4% (0.0436), 2.1% (0.0212) and 26.0% (0.2596) are acceptable roundings, but 'written as the result gives it' favours giving 3.76%, 4.36%, 2.12%, 25.96%. 26.0% is the one that reads as slightly off; use 26.0% only if rounding is stated. Other counts match. Findings: the convergence paragraph says 'dispersion widened', yet the heading and coefficient are fine; but 'the test gives no sign of catching up' infers direction the text admits is unknown. Cut or hedge that. The text also says 'Countries with high poverty by their own line tend to have high poverty by the international line': acceptable. The section does not answer how headcounts changed; state that plainly in the opening and shorten the repeated disclaimers. The 'Multidimensional' heading says 'comparable course', which overstates; the series differ (peak 2018 against 2021). Rename it. Remove the 'in at least one year' phrasing for 'any year' consistency.

r-w-c02-4-4-elm/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts, but several claims do not follow. (1) Sub-Saharan Africa electricity is called 'the fastest regional gain on the Sub-Saharan scale': meaningless; its 17.2-point gain exceeds every other region's, so say 'largest regional gain'. South Asia's expected 2030 electricity value (114.3542%) is omitted, though it is on track. (2) Rural sanitation: the text says no projection exists, true for the cited facts, but 'South Asia and Europe & Central Asia on track' for electricity and water are unmentioned; Europe & Central Asia is on track in electricity. (3) Sub-Saharan Africa water 'far below the target' is fine, but sanitation levels alone cannot show 'pace'; say so plainly. (4) The final heading 'Proposals follow from the gaps' ends on one line, and the proposals are not stated in the text; add them or cut the heading. (5) Cut 'fastest ... scale'; give the electricity world trend its expected 2030 value, 90.9205%. (6) Say rural sanitation Latin America and Middle East regions also lag.

r-w-c02-6-4-orchard/reviewer.comments: Most figures match their facts, but S1 and S3 have problems. (1) The 81 per cent and 39 per cent rises are not facts. They are flagged as calculated, which is honest, but S1 requires every number to be a fact, so cut them or state only the amounts. The claim that the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan & Pakistan region had the largest proportional rise depends on them. (2) The 60 countries reporting in 2025 is correctly matched to its fact, but its reading as showing a thin base is inference; say only that 60 countries reported. (3) The heading 'Education shares fell in most regions' is consistent with five of seven regions falling. Check that the count of five rests on mixed end years (2022 to 2025), and say so in the heading's paragraph. (4) The text states 2023 as the last year of broad health coverage but 2024's 7 countries is a fact; fine. (5) The proposal on constant prices follows from the current-dollar caveat, but the finding about price effects is asserted, not shown by the data.

r-w-c02-6-4-elm/reviewer.comments: Most figures match their facts, but several do not hold. (1) The claim that the 60 countries reporting in 2025 belong to the education series as a whole is not supported: fact c02-6.r1 gives 60 for 2025 with no series-wide scope, so attribute it carefully or cut the inference about a 'thin base'. (2) The percentages 81 and 39 are derived, not facts; they are flagged as such, but check them: 34.89/19.31 is about 80.7 per cent and 62.29/44.77 about 39.1 per cent, which is acceptable. (3) 'Five of the seven regions fell' is wrong on the figures: East Asia & Pacific, South Asia, North America, Sub-Saharan Africa and MENAAP fell, which is five, but the text lists seven regions while Europe & Central Asia is 'nearly flat', so state it plainly. (4) 'Aid rose in every region' needs North America excluded in the heading. (5) The 136 countries in 2023 and the 2024 count of 7 are fine. Name the 2022 end year for South Asia health consistently.

r-w-c02-5-3-quarry/reviewer.comments: Numbers match their facts: all regional, reporting-count and spread figures agree with the cited values, so S1 holds. Corrections to make: (1) S2: the answer to 'how many affected' is given only as displacement cases; state plainly in the opening that the section cannot give people affected or losses, and say which part of Target 1.5 is addressed. (2) S3: 'Sub-Saharan Africa shows the steepest rise among the large regions' is not supported; Europe and Central Asia rose proportionally far more, and the 2016 start is not comparable. Rephrase to name absolute and proportional rises. 'East Asia and Pacific highest in both years' should be checked; South Asia is second in 2015 but Sub-Saharan Africa is second in 2023, which is fine. 'Where displacing events grew' overreaches given sample change. The proposal on combined regional and national planning rests on a finding the text itself calls cautious; soften it. Cut the reporting-count run (2008 to 2014), which adds little.

r-w-c02-3-4-elm/reviewer.comments: Counts and indices match the facts. Between-region shares are rounded correctly (74.1, 28.8, 21.4 per cent). Problems follow. (1) 'Among the years 2000 to 2023 the peak came in 2018' is supported by the facts. (2) 'Only 17 countries reported in 2022 against 47 in 2018' is correct. (3) 'The count was uneven rather than steadily falling' is fair. (4) The 'related indicator, social insurance coverage' is not among the cited facts; the 2023 count of 1 comes from c02-3.r3, but the text never states what indicator r3 covers. Name it explicitly or cut it. (5) 'In 2015... most of the measured inequality lay between regions; in 2018 and 2021 most lay among countries within the same region' is a correct inference. (6) The 2021 heading 'Dispersion is lower' asserts a trend, which the text itself rejects; soften it. (7) Do not say the 2012 fall to 24 in 2013 is unexplained in two places. (8) Proposal 1 (fixed survey cycle) is not derived from a named finding; tie it to the panel caveat. (9) Gaps section mentions falls after 2018 but the text's causes remain unstated; keep consistent.

coverage-and-recency-indicator-for-natio.name: coverage-and-recency-indicator-for-natio
coverage-and-recency-indicator-for-natio.about: Counts, for each year in a window starting 2015, how many countries have a value in a chosen series, and reports how recent each country's latest survey year is. Intended for national-line poverty series so that missing data can be stated exactly. Aggregates are excluded by using only codes present in the region map.

params.series: World Bank series code to examine, for example SI.POV.DDAY
params.start_year: First year of the window, default 2015
params.end_year: Last year of the window, default 2022
